Achieving universal adoption of federated learning requires addressing privacy concerns related to local datasets. In the context of educational institutions, where data is typically organized by individual schools, a federated learning approach can serve as an effective privacy solution. However, because of the need for model aggregation, a pragmatic vulnerability exists within this model. In FL education, a more privacy-resistent approach involves "hiding" specific local datasets using differential privacy (DP) before aggregation, but due to its costly nature, not all local datasets can be effectively concealed. A compromised participant with access to some shared datasets will incorporate their local datasets while ignoring others to avoid DP expenses. In this paper, we address this issue by introducing the concept of a pragmatic privacy assault (PPA) in federated learning, where a malicious participant strategically conceals their local datasets to perform aggregation more accurately. Furthermore, due to the parallelism of PPA, multiple participants can engage in the process simultaneously. Interestingly, our findings show that even a solitary participant can significantly improve the model's accuracy, while multiple participants involved in PPA can result in substantial degradation of the DP utility. In order to mitigate this issue, we propose a novel defense strategy, referred to as PPA-Res, where participants' training datasets are derived from a shared, centralized dataset, thus reducing the impact of PPA and PPA-Res attacks on federated learning model accuracy.

In a dark matter model where dark matter interacts through a scalar mediator, B meson decays involving a dark baryon-antibaryon pair have additional channels that need to be taken into account. To determine the relevant parameters for these decays, scientists calculate the matrix elements for B decays into a baryon and its antiparticle, using QCD light-cone sum principles. These calculations will provide valuable insights into baryon-mediator dark matter models, allowing researchers to test models experimentally.

In the event of a simultaneous socio-cyber-physical attack on an urban environment, the main challenge lies in effectively managing resources such as defenders, infrastructure, and services, while defending against opposing agents' efforts to cause damage. To address this challenge, we propose an intelligent resource management framework, which leverages deep reinforcement learning to make optimal tactical decisions. By breaking down the complex problem into a hierarchy of sub-decisions, our approach enables agents to independently assess risks, gather empirical data, and scale these learnings to solve varying versions of the problem. We evaluate the effectiveness of our solution by playing against opposing agents in a game-based setting, where our results demonstrate improved performance compared to random strategies and naive approaches.

Researchers have analyzed how black star objects and black holes change phase in low-dimensional systems with a negative exponential potential, finding black star objects can form in the same way they form in conventional anti-de Sitter spaces but are less restricted than they were before.  By studying a specific decoupled limit of the D1-D5 system, this study demonstrates black star objects can transform into black holes in a specific temperature range that was previously thought to be impossible in similar anti-deSitter objects.  To arrive at these findings, this study has applied the path integral approach and identified the key role that the precise arrangement of black star objects plays in their change phase.  This study has also looked at hairless black holes in a specific temperature range that was thought to be impossible in similar anti-deSitter objects and found black holes can form in the same way they form in similar anti-deSitter objects but are more restricted than they were before, and further, this study has shown the exact way in which black holes can change phase.

Text data is susceptible to errors not just from labels but also from the content itself, a problem referred to as general label noise. The consequences of this phenomenon are particularly severe in ranked outcomes, where minor discrepancies can lead to vastly different results. The existing research on handling label noise has primarily been confined to binary classification, leaving the application to other tasks underexplored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a novel approach to mitigate the effects of general label noise on ranked outcomes. The approach is twofold: Firstly, it employs a bag sampling method to identify and remove poorly ranked samples. The quality of these samples is assessed using the predicted ranks from an ensemble of models. The quality threshold is determined by analyzing a quality metric that incorporates pairwise disagreements in predicted ranks. The accuracy of this method is further validated by the invariance of the loss function to the quality threshold. Secondly, it utilizes a group-based asymmetrically weighted loss function to minimize the effects of content-based label noise. The effectiveness of this method has been tested through experiments on the Twitter dataset, where it has demonstrated superior performance over the existing methods under label noise conditions.

The widespread use of Graph Neural Networks in various applications is hindered by the scarcity of pseudo-labels, as conventional approaches to overcome this challenge often require a large dataset, which is rarely available. Unlike previous methods, we propose a different path by rethinking the conventional view of pseudo-labeling. Our proposed method, RePseudo-Tag, employs a novel, multi-faceted approach consisting of four distinct modules: a self-reliant module, an external knowledge module, a self-correcting module, and an adaptive learning module, which collectively overcome the pseudo-label problem without the need for a large dataset. Specifically, our self-correcting module utilizes uncertainty estimation to adapt the quality of pseudo-labels, while our adaptive learning module presents a new perspective on the problem by incorporating the concept of data scarcity. Extensive experimentation across various benchmark datasets confirms our approach's effectiveness compared to both previous and current state-of-the-art methods.

A recent PRL article outlined potential scenarios in which the second operational phase
of AWAKE2 would induce significant levels of hard X-ray emission due to the betatron
acceleration of electrons. This work employs a code for linear-vacuum particle-in-cell
(PIC) simulations to analyze this phenomenon, considering the most likely PIC simulation
scenarios described in the referenced article, and incorporates detailed parameters from
the actual AWAKE2 plasma channel run 2 data. A detailed examination of X-rays produced
during plasma-based plasma-wakefield acceleration was conducted, focusing on regions
where the driving laser is present and where the plasma wave extends beyond its influence.
Additionally, the influence of the driving laser's polarization direction and plasma cell
orientation was assessed, and an estimate of the energy invested in the plasma,
determining the rate at which it loses energy, was calculated.

This paper introduces a new framework for building secure, privacy-focused decision trees in distributed networks. The proposed structure is highly flexible and can be adapted to a variety of distributed setups, including a complete tree arrangement where each worker handles a separate subset of the data. A differential privacy mechanism safeguards both server and client data from eavesdroppers, resulting in an accurate and secure decision tree model even in distributed settings. The added verification features ensure accurate data processing to maintain high levels of accuracy. A precision boosting technique is also implemented to provide guarantees on the distance between the final model and the one generated without considering privacy concerns. To further enhance performance, a new optimization strategy is used for efficient evaluation of sensitive data using secure and verifiable cryptographic techniques. The proposed framework's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to both real-world and simulated datasets, resulting in an impressive balance of security, accuracy, and versatility.

We propose a novel method for the distance minimization problem introduced by Titterington et al. in 1989, a problem where the R\'enyi distance is minimized as the divergence measure becomes unbounded, the limit of its parameter goes to infinity. The proposed divergence can be used for a range of purposes, including model selection, hypothesis testing, and distribution classification. The proposed method is suitable for categorical and continuous data, particularly high-dimensional data, by utilizing an efficient and non-smooth optimization algorithm, built on the Bregman proximal gradient approach, to find the optimal distribution. This algorithm converges at a linear rate under strong convexity conditions, while achieving sublinear convergence (at the O(1/k) rate) when such conditions are not met. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method with several simulation examples and real-world data sets.

A statistical framework called chain event networks (CENs) has been widely used for explaining event sequences based on a group of initial states. Although CENs offer potential applications in various fields, their complex nature poses a problem for automatic selection of relevant variables. In response, we develop a Bayesian approach for selecting the most informative networks and initial states by linking CENs to the Bayesian network (BN) framework. Our method outperforms existing selection techniques, and we illustrate its efficacy through simulations and a real-world study of healthcare-related death sequences.

In finite dimensional spaces, we've developed a dynamic system that models an object with inertia and a damper, gradually moving towards the closest point of a set of feasible solutions. This system's behavior is influenced by a time-based function that controls the convergence's rate. When this function becomes infinitely large, the dynamic system's trajectory converges asymptotically towards the feasible set. Furthermore, under specific conditions on another system parameter, this trajectory also converges towards the feasible set's element with the smallest norm. Notably, if this parameter is sufficiently small after a certain time point, both the primal and dual trajectories converge at a rate proportional to $1/t^{(\alpha+1)/2}$ towards the feasible set's element with the smallest norm, even in the presence of noisy data.

All cells in a cellular automata that feature unbalanced local site-exchange rules covered by a periodic barrier will either fluctuate with no predictable pattern or fall into an unbreakable loop, regardless of the initial configuration. The site-exchange model, commonly known as the Exclusion Process, is the most fundamental form of cellular automata. The local exchange model, which allows cells to move in both directions, is the most basic variant of this formula. The goal of this paper is to understand the long-term behavior of configurations in one-dimensional systems and two-dimensional systems formed by the simplest local exchange process model, with sites blocked by a periodic barrier that only allows for one-directional movement. The model's key characteristic is the fact that a robot can only move to the right, and can't move to the left, when it encounters a barrier. The term "unbreakable loop" refers to a repeating sequence of configurations, and "no predictable pattern" refers to a situation where configurations, over time, with an increasing number of changes, will approach a uniform, predictable, and unchangeable distribution across all possible configurations, regardless of the initial configuration. The site-blocking model, similar to the exclusion process, but only allowing for one-directional movement, has been the subject of various reconfiguring, statistical thermodynamic, and open-dynamic studies in the scientific literature. The concept of unpredictability arises from a unique property of this model. The concept of unpredictability can be better

Within the framework of the loTAP model, which posits that kinetic energy contributes a substantial part of the total energy, a superconducting state emerges in materials that experience tensile forces. When a microwave electromagnetic field interacts with these materials, an apparent resistance to a superconducting state arises due to the time-dependent nature of the microwave field. This apparent resistance becomes lower further from the bandgap region and from the band edge where the microwave absorption is highest. As a result, the edge of the superconducting state appears less sensitive to temperature, but rather to doping levels.

This passage discusses a non-smooth method for analyzing the average curvature of shapes. The analysis involves taking the limit of a sequence of functions, which are defined using second-order differences. The key function in this method is $\delta_{2\delta^2} R^2$, where the delta function has a narrow support and a second moment of 2. The article proves that the approximation of average curvature with second-order differences converges to a finite, non-smooth method in the sense of Gamma-convergence. Furthermore, it shows that this method shares several properties with average curvature, including its relationship with curvature from convex bodies, its minimum value for curves, and its lower semi-continuity. These findings are applied to the study of minimizers of two energy functional types: an elastic model and a gradient flow model. In both cases, the approximations, in the sense of Gamma-convergence and weak Lp-convergence, converge to a limit that is defined by minimizing an action functional, where each function is multiplied by the length of its support.

Plant research is growing, yet professional guidance on plant care is often limited to specific species. Most existing resources rely on subjective opinions, lacking scientific backing. To address this, researchers are experimenting with automated plant care, focusing on indoor plants that can be pruned. Current solutions, however, are specialized to a particular plant species, restricting their application. To broaden the scope of automated plant care, this research proposes an AI-driven method grounded in plant biology and evolutionary principles. The proposed approach simulates a virtual environment, utilizing reinforcement learning to develop cutting techniques that achieve desired aesthetic arrangements while considering the constraints of a particular growth regulator. To demonstrate its capabilities, the method was tested to produce a variety of patterns, including geometric shapes and gradient textures, on a particular indoor plant species.

Lehmann-Schramm-Sheffield demonstrated that the SLE process forms a closed loop when combined with an independent Brownian motion on a specific conformal compactification of the complex plane. They used an approach involving the Drinfeld-Sugawara vacuum in 1982 to achieve this consider a closed loop scheme involving only SLEs that mimics this relationship. This involves decomposing a closed loop into sections corresponding to the Drinfeld-Sugawara vacuum state and demonstrates that these segments conform to the properties of quantum disks. While direct quantum disk formulae are complex, an alternative approach utilizing contour integral representations of Drinfeld-Sugawara vacuum wavefunction is employed to derive the required conditions. This derivation involves verifying that the conformal gluing of conformal loop ensembles is consistent with the underlying theoretical framework. Additionally, the document explores an alternate interpretation in terms of the Vandermonde wavefunction, deriving the necessary conditions along the way.

The Image Indicator Standardization Initiative is a coordinated effort within the Global Labor Internet Partnership's framework, which standardizes image-based development indicators across various fields such as agriculture, health, poverty, and education, enabling governments, organizations, and researchers to utilize machine vision for progress monitoring. By promoting image collection harmonization, the initiative facilitates accurate, large-scale image analysis and yields comparable results across countries. A working group is tasked with developing guidelines, best practices, and a repository, as well as coordinating with other groups to promote image-based development monitoring.

The high-spin nucleon and delta resonances are integral to understanding the dynamics of the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction from the nucleon. We found that, except for the $\Lambda(1116)$, their decay products are not substantial contributors to these processes. The narrow resonances, however, mainly affect $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ at lower energies, where their dominance can be seen in the $K^0\Sigma$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction, particularly in the $K\Sigma$ channel. The high-spin resonances are found to have a considerable impact on the $K\Lambda$ photoproduction, where they are particularly dominant at intermediate energy ranges and in the $\mathcal{A}^{(S)}$ and $\mathcal{A}^{(D)}$ amplitudes. The $\Lambda(1670)$ and $\Lambda(1600)$, however, are not substantial contributors to these processes. The high-spin resonances are found to be integral to $K\Lambda$ at high energy ranges and in the $\mathcal{A}^{(D)}$ amplitude, where their importance is particularly noticeable at high energies and low angles.

One critical step in the biometric system's performance is the quality of input.
This study proposes an open-source, high-performance pre-processing pipeline for face detection, encompassing face localization, alignment, and quality assessment.
Utilizing OpenCV as a foundational framework and incorporating cutting-edge methods ensures efficient processing without sacrificing performance.
This approach offers accurate face detection, robustness, and rapid execution, making it suitable for real-time biometric applications.
Furthermore, we demonstrate its application in enhancing the performance of the face recognition system on the MORPH-II dataset.

The long-established idea that curvaton fields can generate a sufficient scale of inflationally produced black holes to trigger a violent explosion, an explosion of the first star, solves the cosmic microwave background problem. However, it's been long assumed that the required curvaton field mass has already been fixed. We show this isn't the case. The proposed black hole distribution can actually be adjusted by altering the curvaton field mass, which in turn influences the magnitude of tensor mode contributions to the power spectrum. Consequently, the cosmic microwave background constraint concerning isocurvature tensor modes can be somewhat relaxed. Furthermore, we provide new evidence suggesting that the particle nature of the old black hole mass is not fixed.

This research applies a dynamic latent variable model to analyze the educational pathways of a cohort, specifically examining the degree completion rates of the Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction's data from 2016-2017. Our investigation incorporates demographic characteristics into the modeling process, aiming to forecast degree attainment probabilities and demographic associated factors. The results indicate that specific demographic attributes significantly influence degree completion, with varying degrees of influence across different majors. Our analysis suggests that a latent variable model, including time intervals, effectively captures underlying degree completion patterns within a Markov chain without requiring direct observation, providing more accurate results than traditional models.

The simultaneous assessment of vehicle platoon assembly for multiple cars is a complex problem, particularly when it comes to efficient execution. To address this challenge, we have developed a comparison-based approach utilizing a continuous function of states, known as the differential contest, to determine when each vehicle should join the platoon. Our method ensures smooth and continuous assembly, and by making the contest function a link between vehicle states and inter-vehicle distances, we have successfully decoupled the assembly trajectories. Our approach's performance is guaranteed by showing that a Lyapunov function exists, which implies exponential convergence of the system's state to a stable equilibrium point. Our proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation results conducted using Dahlquist's method for numerical integration.

The relationship between an explanatory variable and the probability of an event may depend on other variables, indicating non-interaction after conditioning, which can also imply other variables should be included as additional examples. Logistic regression models the relationship between variables, but can fail to accurately represent certain types of phenomena without including interactions. Our study focuses on identifying how to correctly model real-world data involving irregularities. Three different types of non-linear relationships are examined and demonstrated through simulation using the IRIS dataset, showing how conditioning affects these relationships and leading to a solution for logistic regression models to correctly account for such interactions using a data set involving hospital readmission rates and patient health indicators.

Many news outlets hire professional writers to create news headlines, a costly process. To address this a cheaper approach has been developed, where an automated system is trained to create headlines similar to the real ones by analyzing pairs of summaries and headlines. However, this approach has a major limitation - it can only work if a large amount of labeled data is available. To address this, an adapter has been developed which allows the automated system to re-create headlines from new, manually written summaries that were not part of the training process. The system, called HEAD Adapters, was trained using the Summ-Edt dataset and achieved an F1 score of 73%, comparable to the original system trained on a large amount of labeled data and achieved a score of 74%. The proposed method is successful in the task at hand and does not require large amounts of labeled data.

We propose a model for a chiral spin fluid in the form of a two-dimensional, quantum-disordered Heisenberg antiferromagnet with a term that breaks its spatial and time-reversal symmetries but preserves its chiral rule. Our investigation using two types of Monte Carlo simulations, targeting amorphous and polycrystalline realizations, reveals a unique order parameter that's robust in value, and the system exhibits unique behavior, including a critical temperature that's significantly lower than the system's chiral ordering temperature, and a complex order parameter that's comparable in value to the order parameter for chiral ordering and the system's magnetic susceptibility.

The increasing capabilities of large-scale radio telescopes are crucial for advancing our understanding of the universe, particularly in the search for potentially habitable exoplanets. To effectively utilize these large instruments, new methods of polarimetric calibration are required, which can efficiently handle large numbers of antennas arranged in a two-dimensional grid. This study develops and compares various algorithmic calibration methods, which are capable of scaling efficiently as more antennas are added. By applying calibrations that account for complex antenna interactions and grid-based correlations, our research finds that certain methods, such as a modified maximum-likelihood algorithm, perform nearly as well as the current industry standard while significantly reducing computational demands. This method leverages fast algorithms that can quickly solve complex mathematical equations arising from large antenna arrays and achieves optimal computational scaling. Consequently, our proposed algorithm is seen as a promising alternative to the established methods, making it suitable for upcoming large-scale telescopes aiming to explore exoplanets with interferometric imaging.

A key factor that influences investment decisions, specifically asset allocation, is fundamentally driven by risk and return. Our research, which focuses on yield products, utilizes numerical simulations to examine the risk-return models of yield products. In the course of the research, we encountered issues related to overfitting and a lack of evaluation of risk. To address these problems, we have developed a groundbreaking autoencoding conditional GAN model, which can handle a wide variety of risk-return scenarios learned through an encoder. Notably, this novel model achieves overfitting-resilient results without relying on regularization techniques, thereby outperforming traditional conditional GAN models significantly.

In this study, we have calculated the polarized transition matrix element $A_{gq}(N)$ for $q = \gamma$, $q = q$, and $q = q^\dagger$ within the framework of the variable flavor number scheme up to $O(\alpha_s^3)$. Moreover, we derive double generalized parton transform formulas for $A_{gq}(N)$ and compute its numerical values. Our findings reveal distinct behaviors for $A_{gq}(3)$ under $q$, $q^\dagger$ evolution and demonstrate a clear dependence on the factorization scale $\mu_F$ and $N$. Furthermore, $A_{g\gamma}(N)$ exhibits compositeness at the quark threshold $\mu_F = m_q$ for $\mu_F < m_q$ and $\mu_F > m_q$.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have made it possible to automatically classify Fermi-LAT blazars by leveraging both the time variability patterns and energy spectra of gamma-ray light, observed by multiple blazar monitoring programs. However, these methods have been limited in scope to the Fermi-LAT dataset and a small set of pre-labeled events, restricting their applicability. In contrast, this research employs a Bayesian neural network to classify Fermi-LAT dataset events without pre-labeled events, and compares the results with those from a conventional maximum likelihood method. Furthermore, this classification framework is utilized to investigate the statistical properties of gamma-ray light emitted by flaring blazar candidates, and identifies notable disparities between their and non-flaring blazar populations.

The rapid expansion of social media platforms has significantly enhanced the possibility of inclusive participation, a factor that is crucial for amplifying voices often overlooked in various sectors. To achieve a truly inclusive environment on social media, accessible content must be readily available. For instance, visually impaired individuals require audio descriptions to understand the visual aspects of a post, such as infographics on Facebook. Despite the well-documented challenges in accessible content creation, specific obstacles on social media remain understudied. To address this, a study was conducted on creators with disabilities, and the findings are presented as general recommendations as well as platform-specific suggestions to foster accessible content creation.

This paper explores the concept of tensor hypergraph unions and their spectral properties. We investigate the conditions under which the largest eigenvalue of a hypergraph tensor is equal to its index, and how this relates to the reducibility of null-null tensors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectrum of the union of hypergraph tensors is equal to the set union of the individual spectra, and that their eigenvalue multiplicities add up. By employing specific examples and lower bounds for eigenvalues in k-uniform k-partite k-graph tensor families, we arrive at a crucial result via minimality induction.

The Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) is a 1.25m space-based telescope designed to revolutionize astronomy across various domains, particularly benefitting Indian researchers, by enabling unprecedented observations in multiple wavelength ranges, including blue to near-infrared. To fulfill its ambitious scientific goals, INSIST is equipped with cutting-edge imaging and spectroscopic capabilities. To showcase INSIST's unique selling points, a demonstration mission called INSISTDM is being developed to validate its capabilities in observing distant celestial objects, including the atmospheres of nearby exoplanets and comets. With its groundbreaking capabilities, INSIST will significantly advance the field of astronomy, opening up new frontiers for research.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's, various biomarkers and outcomes are measured,
often displaying complex nonlinear trends in response to disease progression.
To address this, appropriate statistical techniques are essential to accurately
assess treatment efficacy, and our research focuses on a method using natural cubic
splines to analyze multiple outcomes in randomized trials. to demonstrate its
utility, we have applied this approach to the ADNI study in a case study format.
Our method can also be implemented through an easy-to-use R package called NCSSplines.

This paper leverages the H\"{o}rmander-Legendre method, combined with prior $C^{2,\alpha}$ estimates derived from regularity theory, to establish the parabolic L^{\infty} approximation for complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations with l^p Dirichlet data, addressing a long-standing challenge in the field and filling a critical gap in the current literature.

We've developed a strongly normalizing extension of the lambda calculus with a type system, whose computational capabilities are restricted to total functions within a specific category: strictly regular functions involving specific symbol subsets. The strategic choice of foreign functions serves as a mechanism to enforce stronger normalization properties in the type system, thereby serving as an effective teaching tool. By incorporating additional strategies, we can further narrow the computational power of the type system to strict substrings within the category of regular functions. A natural integration of this approach with the term rewriting system, together with specific type restrictions, enables the construction of a proof assistant dedicated to regular string identities. Additionally, our work addresses previously unanswered questions in the theory of word rewriting, particularly concerning the completeness of the completion process aimed at proving non-collapse in arbitrary algebraic systems.

When solving stochastic differential equations, we can define a corresponding ordinary differential equation by replacing the white noise in its input with a colored noise that satisfies specific requirements. We call the resulting solution a conditional distribution flow. When these flows are used in an Stratonovich integral, this integral obeys Chen's formula. This formula has two key properties: it is invariant under changes in the representation of the flow and it preserves the geometric property of being a string equation. These results have two important applications: first, we can show that an Itô integral representing the same string equation can be expressed in terms of the conditional distribution flow and its derivatives; second, we can find a specific form of colored noise that converts an Itô differential equation into an equivalent Stratonovich differential equation with a Stratonovich integral that is invariant under changes in the representation of the flow.

A discrete group's topology is the finest, with its closure under all locally determined topologies sharing the same Hausdorff property, known as the standard space of the group, with notable examples including the Bohr compactification of the abelian group and the largest compactification of the semigroup, with various algebraic and functional consequences.

Current text-to-SQL models face two significant challenges: they are often trained on one dataset and tested on another due to the scarcity and high cost of labeled data, and they lack a parser that can break down the text into comprehensible SQL components. To address these issues, we propose a cross-dataset approach utilizing domain-specific pretraining and incorporating an auxiliary SQL generation task that learns from both training and testing datasets, and we further develop a parser that generates interpretable SQL queries with the aid of SQL token classifiers. Our experiments on three real-world databases reveal the advantages of our strategy in handling domain shifts and producing understandable SQL queries.

In the realm of Multi-Robot Systems, managing collision risks is crucial.
Typical approaches rely on either static models of robot dynamics or assume access to accurate predictions of future states. 
Unfortunately, future predictions are often inaccurate, especially with multiple robots moving simultaneously, and errors can escalate with time due to dynamics uncertainty. 
To mitigate this issue, this research proposes a novel risk-averse model predictive method that incorporates recent observations, making it robust to forecasting errors. 
This framework is based on Multi-Robot Risk-averse Model Predictive Navigation (MiRiN), a novel approach. 
MiRin produces collision-free paths even without knowing the true dynamics of robots, as it develops and applies this framework within the Stanford Humanoid Lab. 
This research also outlines key implementation considerations, presenting both simulation and real-world experimental results, demonstrating MiRiN's ability to navigate safely through crowded scenarios, even with inaccurate future predictions.

A recent discovery of an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy, Andromeda XXV, necessitates a detailed examination for reliable characterization. Andromeda XXV, visible as a point-like galaxy, was detected at a distance of 850 kpc from our home galaxy, primarily through its low metal content and distinctiveness in its host environment, compared to similar galaxies in the Milky Way and M31 halos. Its population of old stars, with a low dark matter density at its center, makes it unique. These properties, along with a notably low tidal heating rate, place Andromeda XXV among the smallest known galaxies. Its internal dynamics, particularly those influenced by tidal forces, suggest it is relatively undisturbed. These findings contribute to our understanding of dwarf galaxy formation and galaxy-galaxy interactions.

A dual-stage approach has been developed to create non-orthogonal patterns (NOPs) for grant-free massive connectivity systems. In the initial phase, sparse NOPs are designed using a dual-stage genetic algorithm (DUGA) to minimize NOP length, peak-to-average power ratio, and the count of non-zero elements, while taking into account the maximum auto-correlation and cross-correlation values. A multi-objective selection pressure mechanism is employed in DUGA to handle these interdependent objectives. A DUGA method called SP-DUGA is particularly effective for generating NOPs with a small number of non-zero components, enabling grant-free connectivity in IoT networks. In the second stage, dense NOPs are derived from the sparse patterns using a dual-stage genetic algorithm called DG-SP to their sparse counterparts. A dense NOP is designed using SP-DUGA if it achieves lower peak-to-average power ratio, better auto-correlation properties, and cross-correlation performance, along with a lower count of non-zero components. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed dense patterns outperform Gold sequences, SLC-SPC codes, and a machine learning-based dense NOP generator known as NPOM, achieving up to 2 dB performance improvement over the best competing scheme across multiple key performance measures such as peak-to-average power ratio, average cross-correlation output, and average auto-correlation output

The accuracy of computer models relying on the Maxwell-Stefan approach for multicomner gas diffusion is evaluated using energy conservation and the Gibbs-Duhem equation. The results of this evaluation indicate that the internally consistent applications of this approach lead to a positive definite diffusion coefficient matrix, ensuring stability. Several theoretical examples are employed to illustrate the theoretical framework for numerically computing flux based on the Maxwell-Stefan approach. One scenario illustrates its theoretical feasibility for accurate predictions of gas diffusion in practical settings, namely, the exchange of humid air. Calculations demonstrate that approximation-based methods can yield substantial errors in their predictions of gas diffusion, which may reach up to 10% compared to more accurate models. The implications of these findings for experiments designed to validate models of multicomponent gas diffusion are also discussed.

We define, for each matroid, an associated outer algebra that expands traditional linear algebra by leveraging matroid theory's properties in a natural way. This outer algebra's elements and operations are built upon fundamental concepts such as local connectedness, local trees, and the connection to major linear algebra tools like Gaussian elimination and row and column spaces. This framework's advantages are demonstrated through its application in matroid statistics and the development of a geometric lattice related to symmetric polynomials.

In tasks such as dialogue management and food ordering, accurately interpreting user requests is crucial, but user inputs can be hampered by recognition errors. We propose a method that leverages a neural automatic speech recognition system's uncertainty to predict the dialogue state, by exploring the system's uncertainty through a word confusion network derived from the system's output. This method captures the relationship between recognition error patterns and the dialogue state, utilizing a model trained on confusion networks to facilitate uncertainty augmentation. We validate our approach using the SLIM-Dialog dataset in both simulated and real environments, demonstrating improved performance over traditional methods that rely on raw audio inputs.

The enumeration achieves this goal through the development of a function field analogue of the K-theory of the Hilbert scheme, drawing upon collaborative efforts between I. M. Kedlaya and X. Liu regarding the p-adic Hitchin system, as presented in their respective papers.

We introduce a novel technique for efficiently quantifying entanglement in complex optical states, capable of handling multiple modes and-gates. This elegant method leverages optimized measurements to produce the quantum Bell inequality, allowing for the unambiguous verification of non-local correlations. Our approach is experimentally validated using maximal mixed states, marking a crucial step towards real-world applications of optical quantum computation.

Palm Tree Modes (PTMs) have been detected in the core of JET's discharges with low plasma current. The discovery of PTMs in core regions is atypical, as these mode types are generally observed at low shear in edge regions. Investigative analysis of the local magnetic field structure and detailed mode frequency scans reveal that the discovery of PTMs is connected to a twisted magnetic field topology characterized by (5,10) rational surfaces. The study further demonstrates that this twisted field structure is connected to a localized area of very low magnetic shear, rather than directly resulting from it. The fluctuation profiles show that the radial component of PTMs has two distinct peaks, surrounding the central plasma area, indicative of two separate magnetic X-points. The identification of these X-points serves as a reliable diagnostic tool for determining the Rational Surface Location, or RSLL, of trapped magnetic surfaces. The research also implies that reconstructing magnetic field using external magnetic probes is essential for accurately identifying the Rational Surface Location, as this is crucial for understanding and interpreting PTMs. The effect of twisted field structure on electron density and electrostatic potential profiles is discussed in this study.

Pretrained models, which are trained on large, extensive datasets, have revolutionized computer vision. Their success stems from two key factors: the advancements in deep learning and the utilization of extensive pretraining on vast datasets such as ImageNet. Following the emergence of self-supervised learning, researchers have successfully adapted these models for unsupervised training objectives. However, their application is heavily reliant on fixed architectures and predetermined parameter settings, which must be carefully chosen before the learning process begins. This requirement poses a significant challenge in implementing these models in settings of continuous learning and deep reinforcement learning, which often come with limited budgets and uncertain reward functions. To address this limitation, we introduce the SOBEL benchmark, which evaluates pretrained models within the confines of continuous learning. Our findings suggest that no single approach currently dominates, and SOBEL presents an avenue for further investigation.

The surge in social media usage has facilitated a rapid spread of harmful content, particularly hate speech, which uniquely combines visual and textual elements. While machine learning techniques have achieved a certain level of success in identifying purely textual hate speech, they fall short when dealing with multimodal hate speech due to its subtle nuances and complexity. This paper presents an innovative approach to identifying such content by leveraging the capabilities of pre-trained visual and text transformers to efficiently integrate and analyze image and text inputs from image-text pairs and multi-text posts respectively. Furthermore, we propose a multi-task learning framework that utilizes two key tasks: a binary classification task to detect hate speech and a multi-class task to identify its specific target, which also helps boost the model's performance through feature sharing, weight sharing, and regularization. We evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on the EmorSeH dataset in a comprehensive manner, observing an improvement of 4.1% in the F1 score and a enhancement of 10.2% in the AUC over the baseline models.

Neural networks, specifically those composed of Type-I neurons, are widely studied in various contexts due to their ability to produce repetitive signals. In natural settings, these networks rarely exist in isolation, influencing one another and thereby affecting their rhythmic activity. This paper explores the synchronous behavior of Type-I neurons within random networks under the mean-field approximation, with a focus on the distribution of neuron response times. By investigating the general case, the study delves into the impacts of varying decay parameters, and specifically examines the case of the Weibull distribution used to model neuronal firing in the Hodgkin-Huxley system. It is crucial to accurately account for the distribution of response times to accurately predict the behavior of such networks in real-world scenarios.

Our proposed technique allows machine learning models to generate antagonistic patches, which highlight coding mistakes contrary to the intended functionality. By training an automated learning model on a dataset comprising human-created patches that resolve bug-free programs in accordance with these programs' specifications, our approach generates counterexamples where the programs in question fall short. The instance where the model identifies a low-scoring antagonistic patch signifies a program developer's coding mistake. The antpatch method was successfully applied to an established program repair system and resulted in a 9% enhancement in success rate when integrated with this system. The model's performance in detecting program errors is also evaluated through an examination of high-performing antagonistic patches created for well-known bugs in open-source projects.

A data spectrum has been proposed to explore the capability boundaries of geometric Innes-type fully coherent states in regions where their properties deviate from those of Geogen-Bargmann states. An examination was conducted on the energy distribution and entropy of data spectra for GIFC with complex Gaussonian parameters. Notably, GIFC were found to retain characteristics similar to Fock states up to square root order levels and also retained those similar to Coherent States (CS) at a higher level, albeit to a lesser extent. Furthermore, a type of self-organization was observed in the capability regions of GIFC.

A new three-dimensional analysis tool has been created to study fluid behavior using Monte Carlo simulations without interactions. By breaking down the equation-of-state into a series of flow-specific components and employing a flow-specific random solver, the new approach yields more precise solutions. It's capable of simultaneously determining key parameters in the liquid's equation-of-state from observations of its surface tension and bulk oscillation frequencies. The effectiveness of this novel method is demonstrated by applying it to various flow models: the van der Waals and Redlich-Kwong equations, for which it generates accurate predictions when compared to their original parameters. It's particularly useful for investigations into critical phenomena, where traditional examination techniques fail or require extensive knowledge of the flow model's underlying structure.

Deep learning-based approaches have effectively applied to computer vision problems early in the COVID-19 outbreak, and further advancements in this field could lead to advancements in public health services. However, current models have a significant issue of vulnerability to adversarial attacks, and many have been trained using clear images, which are easily manipulated and result in inaccurate outcomes. It's also been discovered that models trained on clear images can't adequately secure sensitive data, which can be recovered by attackers using insights gained by examining the images' associated gradients. Due to these challenges, our study proposes a new method, which leverages a traditional contrastive loss to create a new type of training data, which is more resistant to adversarial attacks and more secure for training datasets. Our proposed method, which utilizes CNNs, has shown better results against adversarial attacks compared to other models by 11.5% in our testing, which revealed that COVIDNet achieved an accuracy of 99.22% in identifying COVID-19 cases, which outperforms other models.

The growing reliance on wireless communication systems necessitates an increase in both efficiency and adaptability.  Decentralized systems employing graph-based protocols offer a viable solution to enhance the interconnectivity of these systems and enable various applications, such as task scheduling and resource allocation.  However, given the dynamic nature of wireless communication systems, existing graph-based methods are inadequate due to their inability to cope with changing conditions.  In an effort to address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that leverages the potential of graph-based systems while leveraging the computational capabilities of machine learning, specifically a Graph Neural Network (GNN), in a decentralized architecture.  Our novel approach enables each node in the graph to process and update its local information using the GNN, and then make informed decisions on its communication strategy based on the updated graph.  In various benchmark testing scenarios, including wireless task scheduling, our results demonstrate that this novel decentralized framework achieves a high level of adaptability, outperforming existing methodologies in terms of energy efficiency.

A statistical analysis was conducted on the annual count of homicide cases in 220 municipalities across Goias, Brazil, spanning the period from 2002 to 2014. Our analysis incorporated data compilation methodologies, population rates, and available case counts, along with statistical significance testing for spatial autocorrelation and spatial clusters. The outcomes indicated no significant spatial clustering in the individual county data sets or the aggregated data set. However, significant spatial autocorrelation and clusters emerged in two specific periods: 2002-2006 and 2007-2014. In the first period, two distinct clusters were found: one with high homicide counts and another with low counts. In the subsequent period, only the high-count cluster persisted. Furthermore, significant spatial structure and clustering were observed in the count of distinct types of crimes: theft, arson, and drug-related crimes.

Our study conducts a mathematical evaluation of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) dynamics under real-world data conditions, which are characterised by high challenge levels, non-convexity, and outlying data points in specific regions. As such, we examine SGD from a perspective that prioritises its ability to navigate between these challenging areas and local minima. Building on this perspective, we develop novel optimisation algorithms that are more effective than traditional SGD, capable of balancing exploration and finding local minima. We specifically consider two stochastic gradient approaches - Gradient Accumulation and Gradient Acceleration. GA achieves a balance by combining multiple gradients from larger steps with single gradients from smaller steps. GE, on the other hand, uses larger step gradients for faster progress in lower-curve areas and smaller step gradients for finer adjustments in regions closer to minima. We test the performance of these methods against standard SGD and find that they significantly enhance generalisation performance, even at local minima. We verify the reliability of these methods by applying them to a variety of non-convex learning tasks, including binary classification using different datasets, training of recurrent neural networks, and reinforcement learning using on-policy learning.

A widely accepted understanding of self-exciting systems centers around a stable equilibrium that's repeatedly disrupted by external impulses, with new patterns emerging from these disruptions. However, in this paper, we challenge this conventional understanding by introducing a new type of self-exciting system, characterized by distinct features. Unlike traditional models, our new framework does not rely on impulse-driven impulse generation, instead featuring only one fundamental building block. Moreover, we explore how varying levels of 'coarse-graining' affect the emergence of novel patterns within these systems.

Developing successful manipulation and manipulation learning is a significant challenge for robots. In comparison to humans, they struggle to apply their experience in object recognition and grasp planning. Recent advancements have been made with simulated generation methods that enable the exploration of various grasp configurations. Nevertheless, conventional approaches fail to consider a wide range of possible grasps. Our solution, a system for simulating grasp execution using a universal tool on objects with diverse shapes and sizes, is proposed to address this issue. By incorporating a parallel structure for simultaneous simulation execution and sensor data collection, we demonstrate the feasibility of developing high-quality datasets. By employing a grasp generator to create an extensive repertoire of grasps and executing them using a software-based system that considers various environmental factors, we have successfully created a dataset of dexterous grasp configurations. By filtering out geometrically invalid grasps, we have reduced the initial pool to 10,000. A robotic arm is then used to acquire depth images of 20,000 objects, which are fed into a deep learning-based grasp generator to obtain grasp configurations. Our system successfully achieves an 85% success rate with a delay of 0.7 seconds, demonstrating its potential in demonstrating advanced manipulation skills. By filtering based on grasp execution outcomes, we have obtained a dataset of 8,000 high-quality grasps across diverse shapes and sizes. Additionally, we have proposed evaluation metrics, such as success rate and success distance, to assess the effectiveness of grasp execution

Image quality of free-breathing four-dimensional MRI, used for monitoring respiratory motion, is compromised due to movement artifacts and signal loss. This issue is overcome with the development of a novel MRI sequence, referred to as Motion-Adjusted MRI (MaMRI), which enhances the clarity and resolution of such images. The research presents a unique fast MRI technique, MaMRI2, that was optimized and applied for imaging the thorax and abdomen in humans. The technique was compared to a turbo spin-echo reference sequence in terms of various image quality metrics, revealing MaMRI2 to significantly improve spatial and temporal resolution, overall signal strength, and signal-to-noise ratio, while also reducing distortion and artifacts. The application of a deep learning-based denoising method, named Patchwise Deep Denoising (PdDD), was then utilized to further improve the quality of MaMRI2 images, resulting in increased signal strength, extended field of view, and extended MRI coverage. The PdDD images were successfully used to diagnose lung cancer and liver metastases, and were further analyzed to quantify the effectiveness of radiotherapy in patients undergoing treatment. The research demonstrates the potential of MaMRI2 and PdDD to produce clear and informative MRI images for the diagnosis and monitoring of respiratory motion in MRI imaging.

Our proposed method preserves data flow through knowledge distillation (KD), aiming to utilize a compact model to replicate the input-output behavior of its larger, more complex counterpart. This approach combines two distinct forms of supervision. Firstly, the primary reduction strategy relies on distilling the outputs of the primary data flow in the target network, alongside the standard output results. Secondly, to capture side data flow in the network, we employ gradient matching in the target network, ensuring a closer representation of the learning dynamics. To summarize the distilled information from these data flow paths, we use two distinct methods. One involves employing a principal component analysis (PCA) layer to condense the data, while the other uses self-supervised learning to extract intrinsic patterns from the data. Our approach on model reduction via KD demonstrates superior results on image classification, achieving greater accuracy and more efficient neural networks. The approach also yields better performance when applied to tensor compression.

Our study demonstrates that a generic smooth projection from the plane to a single number dimension creates non-smooth layers that are locally and smoothly similar to the levels of a smooth function without critical points, divided into separate sections by this projection. Each continuous section of this projection has a corresponding topological model smooth projection. Moreover, we show that these continuous parts of a non-linear projection can be smoothly topologically equivalent to parts of a linear projection from R^2 to R, where linear projections also have their linear level curves at the origin where derivatives are defined without losing smoothness under the projection.

In desert landscapes, water is the determining factor for plant growth, and their proximity to water sources is crucial for their survival. Plants' roots can draw water from various distances, and this non-local movement of water is a key aspect of plant behavior. This study uses a mathematical model to simulate an average water supply and its varying distances to plant locations, taking into account an underlying stochastic process that simulates real-world water distribution. The results of the simulation show that plants thrive best when supplied with an average level of water and are more resilient in wetter environments. Sensitivity analyses indicate that higher levels of water availability and lower rates of water consumption lead to the most efficient use of water by the plant community, and consequently, lower average distances to water sources are ideal for plant growth.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique, the CountSketch data structure, is commonly used for approximate frequent items estimation in large datasets, providing reliable results with guaranteed accuracy. However, previous study of CountSketch revealed vulnerabilities to malicious inputs that cause inaccuracies in estimation. In response, a resilient variant of CountSketch was proposed by incorporating an outlier detection method. In this paper, we evaluate the countSketch's performance under specific adversarial scenarios, namely white box and black box attacks, and propose a more robust outlier detection method, the robust CountSketch, that can withstand these attacks and, in certain cases, outperform the previous variant. Furthermore, to increase the security of CountSketch, we also suggest integrating it with the principle of differential privacy, and, in addition, we develop two M-estimators for CountSketch to increase its resistance to adversarial attacks, and, in a certain case, outperform the previous M-estimators.

A cutting-edge version of the auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) method, implemented through the ipie package, has been created and optimized for both central processing units (CPUs) and graphical processing units (GPUs). This sophisticated software module boasts an adaptable and efficient implementation, facilitated through python's straightforward and flexible interface, allowing for seamless integration with other programs and the use of its extensive libraries. To optimize performance, ipie incorporates advanced, low-level operations, allowing for the efficient distribution of GPUS and efficient management of CPUs. This article details the underlying principles and technical aspects of ipie, along with showcasing its applications in predicting electronic ground states of small and transition metals, and the prediction of a novel high-temperature superconductor.

This paper explores two classic game theory scenarios -- the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Tragedy of the Commons -- through quantum mechanics-based simulations that leverage cloud-based quantum systems. Traditional game theory relies on classical strategies, but with the advent of quantum computing, there's a need to develop equivalent quantum strategies for these games. Our groundbreaking simulation of the Prisoner's Dilemma leverages real-time data from cryptocurrency markets to inform quantum strategy adjustments, achieving a higher payoff than anticipated by game theory predictions. Achieving this outcome requires continuous adjustments based on frequent real-world events and real-time quantum strategy modifications. However, current quantum hardware limitations, specifically in execution time and re-initialization processes, impose a minimum time interval between these adjustments. As a result, our experiments revealed a significant discrepancy between game theory predictions and actual results, with quantum strategies falling short. To overcome this limitation, we've devised an elevated frequency trading strategy that outperforms game theory predictions by exploiting cryptocurrency market trends, resulting in a 20% increase in payoff. This requires real-time adjustment of quantum strategy based on timely real-world data, specifically from the trading of Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
I reveal a relatively simple, yet effective strategy for achieving optimal revenue in situations where intermediaries are involved.

To create a comprehensive understanding of a document, we rely on plain text descriptions which must accurately capture its core ideas.  However, finding a suitable keyword or phrase in a document's content to substitute with in a summary can be an arduous task.  In this study, we've developed a plain text summarization system incorporating keyword prompts to substitute with in the output.  First, we redefined text summarization as a decision-making process, or plan, to choose relevant sentences.  Next, we proposed a new type of prompt called acquired entity prompts which facilitate easier, more precise comprehension of a document, and higher quality text replacements in the output.  Furthermore, we designed a learning approach to determine the optimal path of choosing relevant sentences called dynamic partial mapping.  Our results show that acquired entity prompts outperform previously known plainer text prompts which result in better quality text descriptions generated by a machine learning model, and our results with human evaluators confirm that acquired entity prompts lead to more accurate and higher quality text descriptions generated by a machine learning model, and our results with human evaluators confirm that acquired entity prompts outperform previously known text promotion methods, resulting in better quality text descriptions generated by a machine learning model.

This note introduces a new concept of differentiability for functions of multiple variables and uses this idea to present a straightforward proof of differentiability for a function, given that related functions of one variable differ only in a small amount.

Researchers have established a link between vocal variations and visual synchronized movements, which is known as ensemble. In the realm of human-computer interaction, developing autonomous agents that can control speech patterns dynamically is a key focus. However, the existing evaluation methods for this, often based on turn-by-turn analysis, fail to account for the significance of dialogue context. This paper introduces a new context-aware vocal entrapment algorithm and tests it through automatic evaluation in scripted dialogues. The results demonstrate that the new approach yields more accurate outcomes compared to the existing context-independent baseline. Additionally, the method's non-stationary results highlight the difficulty of accumulating evidence across the entire dialogue history, which machine learning models may struggle to capture.

Within the framework of unitary sphere models, our research leverages a global U(1) symmetry to parameterize these models based on a spherical decomposition of large N Hilbert spaces into irreducible U(1) components. By introducing a unitary operator that incorporates this U(1) phase, our approach achieves a diagonalization of Hamiltonians in each component space. Subsequently, we demonstrate how the interplay of 't Hooft's Lambda-S_1 method can be adapted to these models at the finite N level, resulting in a matrix-valued evolution across the decomposition spaces. A key achievement of our work is the successful extension of a tensor category approach developed by Baez and Vicary to the unitary sphere context, providing a rigorous foundation for our results. Additionally, our approach yields valuable insights into the Lambda-S_1 techniques and confirms their equivalence to other methods such as those employed by Bernevig and 't Hooft. Moreover, we investigate the matrix-valued partition functions' behavior in the large N limit and draw upon a spherical Kac-Wakimoto decomposition to extract spectrum information from these functions.

Analytical calculations for two types of quasiparticle disturbances within the fractional quantum Hall regime are conducted in this research. By using the Landau wave function, it's demonstrated that the two-body interaction potential in first order depends solely on the Laughlin wave function's values at specific points. Building upon this finding, we derive an analytical expression for the excitation energy of a quasihole accompanied by a particle created by the lowering and raising operators respectively, relative to the Laughlin ground state. Similarly, we obtain an analytical expression for an excitation energy equivalent to the two-body interaction potential when the distance between electrons approaches twice the magnetic length. These findings are in accordance with previous variational calculations and reveal that, for certain values of ν, we can achieve accurate results for the excitation energy via this two-body interaction potential calculation, resulting in variations less than one percent compared to variational methods.

In the field of mathematical modeling, a semicoercive variational inequality based on a decomposition of ice is proposed, a concept that has been studied in the context of glaciological flow. The given problem exhibits two distinct characteristics - a constraint due to incompressibility expressed through a Lagrange multiplier, and a convective term stemming from the flow's velocity. A unified approach involving FEM spaces of arbitrary order, a perturbation argument, and a specific trace inequality is presented to establish the a priori error estimate for a finite element solution.

A next-generation telescope, DUVET, is proposed to become a space-based, wide-field UV telescope with advanced capabilities. It's designed as a 1.5-meter reflecting telescope, equipped with 2 cameras, to detect star-forming regions in nearby galaxies. It's capable of being launched into a low-Earth orbit with the help of the Japanese H3 launch vehicle and can observe star-forming gas disks in great detail up to 30 megaparsecs. By comparing the UVA and VIS surface brightness, DUVET will be able to identify star-forming regions and their associated feedback mechanisms. It will be able to study how the formation of stars affects galactic evolution, providing valuable insights into the process of galaxy evolution.

In a thorough examination of the multiphase transport model, our analysis of the triangular flow $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Collisions at LHC energies reveals that $v_3$ is highly sensitive to the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma and the phase transition. This sensitivity allows us to constrain critical parameters, such as the critical baryon chemical potential $\mu_B^C$ and the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio at the phase transition $\eta/s|_{\rm MC}$. Based on the measurement of $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}= 2.76$ TeV, our analysis suggests that $\mu_B^C$ and $\eta/s|_{\rm MC}$ must be lower than specific thresholds or else $v_3$ would be higher than observed. Additionally, our investigation of $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions at the same energy in different centrality classes provides further information on the initial state and our results indicate that incorporating realistic nuclear thickness functions significantly enhances the agreement with experimental data.

This research introduces and validates the Simultaneous R-Structure, a concept that employs the cross-section properties of a robot to describe its configuration and motion capabilities. A key feature of the Sim-R structure is that it uses a set of cross-section properties at each point along the robot's body to define its configuration space as a product space. Additionally, a product-space Jacobian framework is proposed, that maps the robot's configuration space to its task space using the cross-section Jacobians at each point along the robot's body. Furthermore, constraints that bound the cross-section properties at each point along the robot's body can be expressed as sums of squares polynomials, enabling the application of advanced optimization techniques to analyze the robot's motion capabilities. As an example, a two-link planar robot equipped with square cross-sections is presented to illustrate the proposed Sim-R structure concept and demonstrate its utility in assessing the motion capabilities of robots with complex configurations.

Deep neural network architectures for semantic segmentation have reached human-level performance, but they still struggle with rare object classes due to a lack of training data. Therefore, researchers are exploring transfer learning techniques, specifically pre-training on complex tasks such as assessing monocular depth perception. The effectiveness of using monocular depth assessment pre-training compared to traditional methods has been investigated. Surprisingly, monocular depth assessment pre-training does not consistently outperform more conventional methods, leading researchers to believe the outcome may be due to the nature of the depth estimation task itself. The evaluation involved analyzing the changes in the feature representation space when using different pre-training methods, but the results did not provide clear insights into the process. The study involved assessing model performance on the ADE20K dataset.

This research enhances the Bohr radius in the context of log-harmonic functions with a log-modulus property resembling starlikeness, by identifying the largest possible radius within the unit disk where function power series remain normal and their absolute values are summable for every function within that class. This result is an advancement of prior work and expands our understanding of Bohr's classical radius in log-harmonic function behavior, particularly in relation to their modulus characteristics.

We introduce the Effective Deduction for Kendall's Tau (EDKT) approach to address imbalanced data, evaluating its effectiveness through accurate table reconstruction using Kendall's tau. We establish a formula and provide bounds for the dismissal parameter d that ensures high accuracy in table reconstruction. We also propose a new metric to measure the level of imbalance and introduce the Effective Discrimination Index (EDI) to compare dismissal methods. Under a balanced design, EDKT achieves similar performance to its parent algorithm, Random Deduction (RD), although it significantly outperforms Uniform Deduction (UD), which has no rejection phase. Furthermore, EDKT generally outperforms other methods in reconstructing tables from highly imbalanced datasets.

In the rapidly expanding world of IoT, the automotive industry is experiencing significant transformations, with self-driving vehicles becoming a major focus. Nevertheless, the current method of training machine learning models using vehicle data poses serious concerns regarding data security and personal privacy protection. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that leverages the homomorphic encryption technique to safeguard vehicle data during the model training process within automotive networks, thereby preventing malicious attacks and leaking of sensitive information. Specifically, we have developed an innovative security framework to overcome computation and storage limitations of homomorphic encryption, thereby enabling efficient secure learning. Our proposed framework comprises an RLWE-based base framework for computation efficiency alongside an RLWINN model inspired by CNNs to optimize storage efficiency. By incorporating an RLWINN framework, we have been able to accurately predict vehicle data, showcasing superior performance compared to conventional centralized learning methods. Furthermore, we have successfully implemented our framework on actual hardware platforms and conducted thorough experiments demonstrating data security throughout the model training process within automotive networks.

This research focuses on a novel method for extracting Euler Significance Surfaces from vector fields, where the complexity of Euler characteristics serves as an importance metric. The algorithm decomposes vector field regions according to their 1D Euler characteristics and extends this technique to identify surfaces in the 2D case. By employing sub-manifold decomposition, the algorithm is generalized to extract n-dimensional objects, and the effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a range of tests. Additionally, the proposed method is applied to a real-world scenario: extracting Euler Significance Surfaces from the airflow around an F1 car, revealing regions of distinct topological nature that provide insight into the system's dynamics.

This research delves into the intricate dynamics between a predator and prey governed by the Holling-Tanner model, with the prey exhibiting Allee effects and all interaction terms considered. We've derived explicit conditions for coexistence, population extinction and stability in the 2D system, and investigated the stability of 3D, 2D and 1D systems as well as their associated limit cycles and equilibrium points. Our study also establishes a mathematical expression quantifying transitions between these states and explores the implications of varying parameters. Finally, we've validated the model through numerical simulations in the anti-Lorenz environment.

Recently, a new iteration method known as aspect pivot (A-Pivot) was introduced and it has shown superior performance in solving linear optimization problems, especially comparison primal-dual methods. Method A-Pivot is an interior point method characterized by a non-standard iteration path, which was designed to ensure a balanced (aspect) basis. In a series of papers starting with \cite{2022MathProgram2022}, it was shown that A-Pivot has a polynomial bound on iteration count and has affine and projective polynomial bounds. In a series of papers including \cite{2022MathProgram2022}, important properties of A-Pivot were studied, including its iteration path, complexity, and reduction in an aspect measure. This work specifically builds upon the findings of \cite{2022MathProgram2022} to provide further insights into A-Pivot's iteration path. It is demonstrated that each iteration of A-Pivot has a strictly positive affine progress bound under certain non-degeneracy conditions. Moreover, it was found that the infinity norm of A-Pivot's last iteration has a linear bound in terms of the problem dimension and has a linear bound under certain non-degeneracy conditions.
