In the study of directed graphs with random orientation, we found that when preferences in connections are taken into account, certain properties that are typical of undirected graphs do not hold, whereas uniform link mechanisms display different results, specifically the phase transition phenomenon occurs multiple times and a new type of component appears.

A Convoluted Neural Network (CNN) is a deep learning model widely used in computer vision tasks. Its primary function is to extract hierarchical image features through a series of filtering operations and then classify an image accordingly. These networks consist of multiple layers of convolutions and activations, where the initial layers capture smaller features and the later layers combine these features to create more complex representations. In our research, we have explored the use of CNNs in an unconventional setting, beyond image processing. We have leveraged an array of 16 antennas and processed the resulting magnitude and phase data using grayscale images, similar to how input images are processed in computer vision tasks. By adapting CNNs to work with this data, we have been able to classify disturbances within the radio spectrum, referred to as wireless disturbances, and demonstrate significant performance improvements, including more efficient feature extraction and reduced overfitting. Our results indicate that wireless disturbances can be more accurately classified when the initial layers of the network have a lower filter count and the subsequent classes have a higher filter count.

A novel spacetime model, known as the Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic string spacetime, has been suggested to describe the gravitational field around an infinite, uniformly moving line mass with a conical defect. Models of this spacetime, based on both static and space-like displacements, have been proposed and are both solution spaces of Einstein-Maxwell equations. A research space-like displacement scenario reveals that a conical deficit is associated with a void in the spacetime structure rather than the traditional reduction in the spatial circumference. Both space-like and time-like displacement models are characterized by inherent conical distortions that rely on parameters associated with the energy content, electric charge, and magnetic flux. A comparison of the static displacement scenario in both space-like and time-like cases has been undertaken and both spaces are both rotationally and translationally invariant. Calculations based on an energy associated with a null displacement scenario have shown that the space-like displacement associated with energy content is less than the time-like displacement associated with energy content.

Every measure algebra can be broken down into simpler components, some of which resemble the standard measure category model more closely than others do. The "closest" components are considered the most typical, while the others are progressively less so. The measure algebra components can even be characterized using a type of distance metric known as the Frolov-Pestov metric.

Measuring the polarization to some degree is crucial in the context of electron-proton collisions involving deep inelastic scattering and the exchange of a virtual photon, particularly when aiming to confirm the coherence of generalized parton distributions. We have investigated the feasibility of this measurement by predicting corrections due to one-loop QCD and tree-level QED. A full experimental setup has been designed for a fixed-target experiment at M200. Our findings suggest that the electron's role in generating a distinctive signal on the proton is dominated by Compton scattering, with an estimated signal rate of approximately 1000 events per second given a specific beam configuration. A novel observable has been proposed based on the differential cross-section ratio that is insensitive to uncertainties in the photon detection system's efficiency and azimuthal angle alignment. A signal significance exceeding five sigma can be achieved within a reasonable timeframe, even with a conservative estimate of generalized parton distribution uncertainty.

Artificial Intelligence has been extensively studied and applied with various methods and structures at different levels of complexity, but its core definition remains unclear, rendering its performance difficult to evaluate and compare. In order to bridge this gap, a theoretical framework is proposed, providing a mathematical structure and performance metrics for computational intelligence systems. Artificial Intelligence is formally defined and standardized within this framework, allowing for the evaluation and comparison of different intelligence systems. The proposed framework categorizes different types of enhanced artificial intelligence systems, including learning, problem-solving, reasoning, sensing, acting, and communication AI. Moreover, a co-evolutionary approach is advocated, suggesting that AI systems and their environments should be adapted concurrently for mutual improvement.

Our research focuses on a specific many-body system, consisting of bosons with both spin and orbital connections in a correlated state, held within a periodic lattice of beams. A magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the plane in which these orbital connections occur. We've discovered, through sub-cooling this system, a two-dimensional lattice at temperatures above absolute zero and utilizing a quantum gas microscope to visualize it, an unusual outcome resulting from thermal fluctuations exhibits a counterintuitive phenomenon, exhibiting a shifted modulated phase. Moreover, our findings indicate that by introducing disorder, this modulated phase displays a particularly fascinating property, exhibiting a hysteresis loop. These observations are supported through a comparison with theoretical calculations, utilizing the dynamical mean-field approach.

Graph theory's most influential achievement, the Four Color Theorem, was proven by Guthrie, Tait, Heawood, and later by the mathematicians Guthrie, Tait, Heawood, and Dirac. Building on this cornerstone concept, researchers have achieved a comprehensive understanding of vertex coloring properties for graphs expressed by finite abelian groups. We establish the degeneracy of graphs expressed by these groups at various levels and establish a chromatic polynomial inequality constraint. Notably, our analysis reveals an intriguing correlation between group order and graph degeneracy, which is subject to certain conditions, with the degeneracy generally increasing as the group order decreases.

We have derived new results in a two-dimensional superconformal field theory theory with N=4 supersymmetry, which is dual to AdS_4 times a particular two-fold cover of a two-torus with a varying two-form, which was a novel solution found recently. By employing the high-temperature and low temperature limits of the path integral approximation, we have successfully obtained the path integral formulation for AdS_4 and obtained the corresponding entropy at high temperatures, which is given by the Bekenstein-Hawking formula, and the associated Cardy central charge, which is c_bar = 12 c_s / T, at low temperatures. This solution provides significant insights into a wide array of phenomena observed at small spatial dimensions and highlights the power of the string theory.

Researchers have been developing novel kernel functions by analyzing mathematical equations in depth, leading to the discovery of innovative Kernels. These newly created Kernels exhibit exceptional properties and successfully challenge existing benchmarks in both similarity and regression tasks. Moreover, empirical studies demonstrate their capability to surpass established Zeta Kernels in various applications, including solving both supervised and unsupervised learning problems, such as nearest neighbor classification, $c$-means clustering, and principal component analysis.

Beam-induced background and noise from residual gas interaction with beam pipes and beam hazing are expected to be significant challenges at future muon colliders, potentially limiting luminosity by causing equipment damage. Research into noise reduction and mitigation is currently ongoing. This study provides an overview of various beam degradation effects, assessing their likelihood and impact on colliders, and discusses strategies to minimize noise from beam pipe erosion and hazing.

We introduce a novel class of differentiable sparseness measures, called regulated regulated optimal transport (RROT), which encompasses an enhanced version of the popular $\alpha$-divergence as a special case. By providing a RROT-based objective function that maintains differentiability and efficiency, comparable to non-smooth alternatives like L1-regression, we enable optimized stochastic gradient descent for a wide variety of machine learning tasks. Our experiments confirm the superior performance of RROT compared to both $\alpha$-divergence and other sparseness metrics for diverse neural network architectures, demonstrating improved performance on image classification, reconstruction, time-series analysis, and multilabel classification, where additional structural insights regarding the target variable's composition can be effectively captured.

Quantum fluids of bosons and fermions display distinct behaviors, influenced by statistics and interaction patterns. The role of statistics becomes apparent at short distances, although it typically manifests strongly. Notably, the behavior of dilute bosonic systems, which often ignore statistics, shows a more nuanced response in certain situations. Our investigation into the Pauli obstruction within weakly interacting Bose fluids, particularly through the Gross-Pitaevskii functional, demonstrates that Pauli exclusion has an emergent role. The behavior of the energy functional converges to a non-analytic form in the limit of zero scattering length, effectively mimicking the behavior of fermionic systems. The scattering length's continuity across the transition point between bosons and fermions implies the persistence of Pauli obstruction in dense phases. Further analysis reveals that the scattering length acquires corrections due to kinetic energy at high densities, behaving as a positive quantity. Consequently, the Pauli obstruction's role becomes prominent, preventing strong boson-phonon interactions and reorganizing the many-body behavior of the system, akin to Pauli blocking, at high densities. The presence of Pauli obstruction leads to the absence of an attractive phonon interaction and modifies the system's behavior, particularly its roton minimum, in a way consistent with expectations based on fermionic systems. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the significance of statistical effects in quantum fluids, particularly for systems previously assumed to be insensitive. The research sheds new light on the relationship between bos

Our research investigated the perception among software developers of the metaphorical issue known as "test odors" within software testing. Through a comprehensive survey targeting professional developers, we discovered that a substantial majority, 85%, recognize test odors as a genuine concern. Notably, a majority of respondents also perceive test odors to be a significant concern within their organizations. Our findings suggest that most developers agree that a refactoring is necessary to address test odors, and most feel a strong desire to eliminate them within their codebase. Our findings suggest that the test odor metaphor resonates strongly within the software testing community, and we provide empirical support for seven out of the ten test odors proposed in the literature. Our research also outlines areas requiring further exploration to refine the concept of test odors.

This paper explores a nonconvex extension of the interior-point algorithm, adapting a work by Tsitsiklis to handle nonconvex optimization problems, including0- and semi-infinite programming problems, with possible uses in combinatorial optimization and global optimization of polynomial functions.

The ongoing interest in building new lepton colliders has created an increased demand for precise event generators that can accurately simulate complex physical processes, such as the production of quarks and leptons in collisions. For such simulations to be meaningful, they must include not only the primary (hard) interaction but also various "soft" processes, like the emission of soft photons or the production of quarks. In order to achieve high precision in these simulations, we have developed the multi-photon Monte Carlo event generator KKMCee, which incorporates advanced features, including the direct production of quarks and a comprehensive simulation of soft photon emissions. Our results demonstrate that KKMCee is highly effective at matching theoretical predictions from QED calculations and providing an accurate representation of various experimental measurements, such as those from the LEP experiments.

Determining inter-beat intervals accurately is a highly relevant task, necessitating novel approaches across diverse fields. The Tiramisu framework, an advanced tool designed for analyzing 1D time-series data, showcases its versatility by effectively resolving the challenge of estimating inter-beat intervals within ECG signals. When compared to established techniques, the proposed method demonstrates a significant error reduction, reaching 0.03 beats, especially on signals featuring low heart rates. The findings indicate that the proposed approach not only outperforms existing solutions, but also surpasses manual expertise. Furthermore, the proposed method boasts considerable versatility, enabling the identification of beats in multi-beat signals such as those found in respiratory signals.

This study introduces a random algorithm for computing the singular value decomposition of high-dimensional tensors, extending a previously established method for matrix decomposition in the Belizari et al. arXiv paper, which failed to converge when the number of passes was less than the tensor rank. Our work develops a Belief Propagation-based algorithm, capable of taking any number of passes into account and always producing the correct singular subspaces after enough passes equivalent to the tensor rank. As a result, we also provide a new, probabilistic proof of convergence tailored for the case of n-order tensors, alongside the standard random algorithms commonly used in the field.

As graphs continue to grow in representation, they are increasingly being used to model real-world scenarios. These graphs are no longer static entities but rather evolve over time, necessitating the consideration of their temporal aspects. Traditional methods for dealing with dynamic networks rely on time-based segmentation, however, they are limited by their inability to capture the underlying dynamics. We present an alternative perspective, where the network is viewed as a three-dimensional space-time manifold. By leveraging advanced techniques from differential geometry and tensor calculus, we develop a novel framework to embed evolving graphs through the tensorial representation approach. Our framework incorporates a cutting-edge method for embedding graphs in 3D, building upon the 3D Graph Embedding algorithm (3DGE). Our findings indicate that this approach can effectively improve embedding results and that it is capable of outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Abdelrhman-AL/3DGE-SpineTree-Approach.

Our investigation into five-neutron halo nuclei, focusing on the $^7$H and $^9$Li isotopes, utilized a three-body model to analyze the unbound nuclei of $^7$H and $^9$Li as clusters consisting of a stable nucleus and two neutrons. To determine the properties of $^7$H and $^9$Li, we considered two possible structures: (n$^5$H) and ($^3$H + d$^2$). By comparing our model with experimental data, we found that the $^7$H and $^9$Li isotopes behave like resonances near their respective thresholds, characterized by narrow widths and logarithmic derivatives. Notably, the calculated properties of $^7$H and $^9$Li are highly dependent on the EMT$_{pn}$ energy density functional, suggesting that different functionals yield distinct predictions. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that $^7$H and $^9$Li are best described as single-body systems, consisting of a $^3$H nucleus surrounded by four and six neutrons, respectively.

This research paper examines the Nirenberg issue on the ball, specifically the Dirichlet problem for highly nonlinear elliptic equations defined by the following equation:

$$
\begin{cases} 
-\Delta_{y}u=y^{2n}K(e^{2u}-|y|^2\Delta y) & \text{for }y\in S^n_{+},\;n\geq 2,\\
u=0 & \text{on }\partial B^n_{+},
\end{cases}
$$

where the domain $S^n_+$ and $B^n_+$ represent the half sphere and the half ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$, respectively. The function $u$ in the equation is interpreted as the second fundamental form $y^2\kappa^{-2}$, with the curvature $K=e^{-2u}$ being the curvature of the boundary $\partial B^n_+$. The research reveals the existence of blow-up solutions for this problem under given conditions. Furthermore, it categorizes the blow-up sequences into two groups: those blowing up at the boundary and those blowing up in the interior. The authors also investigate the existence and non-existence of blow-up sequences blowing up at the boundary. Lastly, the findings are applied to a related problem in the study of the existence of conformal metrics with scalar curvature $K$.

Recent advancements in deep representation learning have been significant, yet they
often rely on pre-trained models or substantial amounts of labeled data, both of
which can be impractical to acquire. To address this challenge, our research
develops a novel, unsupervised deep representation learning technique that
utilizes a straightforward, coherent component at a representation
aggregation level, measured by a modified metric known as the Sinkhorn distance.
Due to its straightforward nature, this distance can be efficiently and quickly
optimized during iterations, enabling faster training. Moreover, our method
naturally extends to semi-supervised settings, as the additional labeled data
can be seamlessly integrated into the training process without additional
complexity. Through comprehensive evaluations on a variety of standard
benchmarks, our method surpasses existing solutions in terms of classification
accuracy.

Regional collaborations among public health bodies in the UK are facilitating COVID-19 contact tracing, yet their impact on regional performance varies, leading to questions about the overall effectiveness. Prior studies focused on technical aspects, like phone number coverage and response times, but these do not directly correlate with the ability to prevent virus transmission within regions. To address this issue, we developed a mathematical model that simulates the spread of the virus within a region, taking into account the regional performance of contact tracing teams, regional differences in population mobility, and the effectiveness of regional lockdown policies. Using data from a previous study on UK COVID-19 and UK Census population data, we find that regional collaboration can hinder the effectiveness of contact tracing and other mitigation measures. Specifically, residents in smaller regions with less ideal conditions are at a higher risk.

Based on the extended V-band image of Melotte 72 from the 2.3m Bok Observatory, we obtained photometry and proper motions for this cluster using a catalogue containing 115 member stars from Gaia DR2. By analyzing these findings in conjunction with a radial density profile and isochrone fitting, we determined key cluster characteristics. Melotte 72's core centre-to-extended boundary lies at a distance of approximately 2.2 degrees, encompassing an area of about 40 square degrees. From Gaia DR2 data, we calculated Melotte 72's distance to be 2.03 kpc and determined its age to be 1.0 billion years. Additionally, we found the cluster's velocity dispersion components along the x, y, and z axes to be 0.73, 0.79, and 2.0 km/s, respectively. Moreover, we calculated the cluster's total mass to be approximately 1000 solar masses using the Mass versus Radius squared relationship. Furthermore, we determined the cluster's horizontal and vertical galactic plane positions to be 203 and 28 degrees, respectively. Lastly, we evaluated whether Melotte 72 exhibits a uniformity across its main sequence using the $\chi^2$ statistic and discovered no notable excess in the main sequence at the cluster's core.

We investigate the average complexity of a randomly generated polynomial system with a specified structure, particularly one where the pattern of non-zero coefficients remains consistent across various realizations but the values of these coefficients are random. Our analysis relies on a newly developed algorithm called multi-Hessian descent, which utilizes the average properties of a key mathematical object to approximate the system's solution space. This approach, initially established in recent research, has been successfully applied in various settings; however, it remains to be validated in the context of sparse polynomial systems, where the linearization process poses significant computational challenges. Our adaptation of multi-Hessian descent reveals the necessity of working with much larger matrices, thus requiring higher moments of the involved distributions. To address this issue, we have recently derived new bounds for these moments, which rely on the combinatorial structure of the polynomial coefficients. Our experiments confirm that the computed expectations accurately reflect the system's actual complexity and demonstrate the feasibility of obtaining significant speedups by exploiting the pattern of non-zero coefficients during the linearization process. Our findings indicate that, for a particular class of polynomial systems, this approach achieves a substantial reduction in computational complexity by leveraging the pattern of non-zero coefficients.

This research focuses on leveraging computer vision technology to facilitate indoor navigation for robots, with a particular interest in indoor scene recognition. Our proposed technique leverages a single image to infer a image scale estimator capable of identifying partial feature points in novel images and automatically calibrating a robot's camera in real-time, thus overcoming limitations posed by image understanding based on fixed parameters. We have developed an image scale estimator using the Chebyshev distance metric, and we validate the proposed method through real-world experiments involving human-supervised robot navigation.

A new reinforcement learning approach for robot learning, particularly in simulation, involves setting up a task where robots can be guided through specific behaviors. This pre-programmed environment allows learners to efficiently acquire desired skills, taking significantly fewer samples to accomplish this compared to traditional reinforcement learning methods. By incorporating a inverse dynamic model, which describes how actions produce results, we can utilize it as a form of reward in reinforcement learning, thereby enhancing the overall learning efficiency. Moreover, our study demonstrates that adding noise to actions in simulations closely mirrors the conditions that robots encounter in the real world, making our learning approach highly successful even when applied to practical robot scenarios.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission is set to significantly advance our understanding of the Galaxy and its star populations by submitting over 10 billion source candidates for final data release. This comprehensive data package will include precise astrometry, photometry, spectroscopy, and rake data for a definitive glimpse into our Galaxy's three-dimensional structure, serving as an unparalleled reference for future research. This article, focusing on the theoretical and algorithmic foundation of GAIA's mission, aims to provide the necessary background to understand the expected Galaxy and solar system data presented in the final data release.

In this study, we present two efficient vertex-dividers, or $v$-partitions, each capable of reducing treewidth to at most $O(n^{1/2+\epsilon})$ while maintaining a constant fraction of the total vertices. The first is an inexact vertex divider inspired by the work of Alon et al., which generates $v$-partitions with $c$ fractions, where $0 < c < 1$ is a user-defined constant. The second is an exact vertex divider that creates $v$-partitions splitting the graph into just two $c$-smaller fractions for $0 < c < 1 - 2\epsilon$. The time complexity for both is $n \cdot 2^{O((k + \log n)/\epsilon)}$. The space complexity of the second vertex divider is particularly impressive at $O(n^{1.5\sqrt{1}})$. The work also introduces an innovative method for constructing small tree-decompositions of k-colliders in sublinear space by building a specific branch-decomposition of the graph's minor. The time complexity of the proposed vertex divider is $n \cdot 2^{O(k \cdot \log n + \epsilon)}$. The work further extends these results to k-cut-vertex-dividers, which are useful in solving k-connected components and k-flow problems. The space complexity of the vertex-dividers can be applied directly to these problems as well.

The application of weighting networks has gained popularity in social sciences, primarily due to their ability to identify and account for cluster heterogeneity. Directed grouping, specifically, identifies the most significant within-group connections to create an asymmetric network model. Multiple interpretation methods have been proposed for groupings in literature, but these are often not clearly distinguished. We provide a clear, unified interpretation framework for weighted networks with directionality, which applies to directed grouping. We establish a set of essential criteria for the validity of directed grouping, which must be met before applying this method. We also discuss the advantages and disadvantages of inferred networks compared to those based on assessments. We provide an illustrative example and highlight future research opportunities.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in authorizing machine learning, specifically ML, to incorporate domain knowledge to improve problem-solving capabilities. Although ML can be authorized to address optimization and decision-making issues, ensuring that it adheres to physical laws remains a challenge. A notable method for authorized ML is the physics-informed neural network (PINN), which has shown success in solving differential equations. However, verifying compliance of PINNs with domain knowledge remains an open issue. To address this issue, a 'a posteriori' evaluation approach is proposed to assess potential violations of domain knowledge after training. A 'a posteriori' evaluation metric based on residual, contact angle hysteresis, and L1-norm is developed to measure solutions' adherence to constitutive models, boundary conditions, and boundary value problems. A generalized evaluation metric in terms of Lp-norm is also introduced, and a generalized generalized error (GGE) is defined. A comparative analysis of GGE and generalized error (GE) for different training methods demonstrates the proposed evaluation method's effectiveness in verifying solutions provided by PINNs.

In infectious disease studies, the concept of aerosol transmissibility is increasingly significant, yet environmental contamination (e.g., surface particles) receives relatively less attention. This review focuses on combining traditional geostatistical methods and recent artificial intelligence techniques to create and analyze models predicting the spatial spread of pathogens in outdoor environments. Geostatistical models, which are in the public domain, adjust for spatial autocorrelation and spatial scales, and are particularly useful for spatial temporal data. On the other hand, artificial intelligence provides a comprehensive and accurate approach to predictive modeling by incorporating non-spatial data features. Our work aims to present and compare various atmospheric contamination models in a unified framework, ultimately facilitating empirical assessments across different settings.

To distinguish the topological Majorana mode from other states, such as the Cooper pair peak and the trivial zero energy state, we have devised a technique that exploits tunneling spectroscopy with a highly resistive electrode. Owing to the tiny size of the Majorana state at the interface, this approach can effectively isolate the various peaks present in such systems. By implementing an Ohmic contact as the tunneling electrode, the various influences on the interfaces can be controlled and the characteristics of the topological state can be identified through distinctive features in the I-V curve. Specifically, the shape of the I-V curve is influenced by the magnitude of resistance at the electrode's interface and the voltage applied across it. Moreover, the method's efficacy in distinguishing the Majorana state from other states relies on the unique dependence of these states on electrode resistance. Specifically, the Cooper pair peak shifts due to changes in electrode resistance, the zero energy state appears only below a certain resistance threshold, and the Majorana state's characteristics are uniquely defined by a combination of a peak and a dip in the I-V curve, with the position of the peak determined by the voltage applied. Furthermore, the method's suitability for identifying the Majorana state is demonstrated through numerical calculations of the I-V curve.

The study of diverse linear bandsits is an established area in both theory and application, covering a wide array of applications in multi-agent and human-robot collaboration. Existing research often assumes homogeneous action sets, whereas our research explores models with heterogeneous action sets and thus diverse action sets. We establish a loss bound for a linear bandits model where two agents share overlapping action spaces, yet possess distinct actions, and develop a more generalized algorithm applicable to this setting. We demonstrate that our algorithm achieves comparable competitive strength to its homogeneous counterpart. Moreover, we apply this framework to a robotic-assisted surgery collaboration scenario, using a synthetic dataset to show that inferring collaborative preferences from observed actions can yield beneficial preferences for both agents' linear models, specifically for a medical collaboration use-case.

Graphene's unique properties stem from its lattice structure, giving rise to a Berry phase and valley Hall effect in its valence band. Researchers have discovered that the orbital Hall effect, influenced by electric field and inelastic scattering, can substitute the valley Hall effect when the Fermi energy approaches the Berry potential peak. The orbital Hall field, generated by this effect, can be measured and controlled, offering insights into orbital degrees of freedom and valley Halls. However, graphene's orbital Hall effect is less efficient than its silicon-based counterpart due to its lower valley control efficiency and high carrier mobility, which makes valley Hall devices less competitive. Despite these limitations, the orbital Hall effect's substitutional relationship with valley Hall effect may reveal new opportunities in understanding and utilizing graphene's potential in valleytronics.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) that utilize reinforcement learning for learning are susceptible to graph contamination, an vulnerability where adversarial inputs are generated by modifying graph topology to mislead the trained model. A prior study on vulnerability revealed that altering just one or two non-critical nodes can lead to significant accuracy decline, and that the most damaging modifications involve removing critical nodes and connecting them to unimportant nodes. However, this study assumed the trained policy remains unchanged during generation of adversarial examples, despite real-world scenarios where defenders may attempt to mitigate damage by refining the policy. Our research investigates contamination of GNNs that utilize reinforcement learning for graph partitioning, and reveals an unexpected result: incorporating a single critical node into an adversarial graph requires a considerable number of additional samples for performance recovery. Instead, we propose that a practical countermeasure for defenders is data contamination, achieved by applying a critical node to an unimportant node, akin to the generation of adversarial examples for deep learning models. Experimental results confirm that this approach substantially reduces the required samples for recovery.

To determine the relative movements of stars, we must compare their positions across two catalogs that are based on data from different sources. In the absence of a comprehensive catalog that accurately tracks the positions of stars in our area of interest, we must rely on data from various sources. We examine the potential of combining data from two catalogs, one that focuses on bright stars and another that is more comprehensive, to understand the effect of this approach. We achieve this by creating two catalogs of the motions of stars in the local region of the Milky Way, one that focuses on the brightest stars and another that includes both the bright and dimmer stars. We incorporate data from two catalogs, one that focuses on the motions of the brightest stars, HD104, and the other, Hipparcos, to create a new catalog of the motions of the stars in the area. We then use a combination of these catalogs to create a comprehensive catalog of the motions of the stars in the area. We demonstrate that by combining the catalogs, we can achieve a comprehensive catalog of the motions of the stars in the area.

We establish a minimum requirement for the cardinality of a set $X$ in an infinite $(k,r)$-uniform hypergraph, such that removing $X$ results in fewer than $\ell$ edges. Specifically, if the hypergraph's edges $\mathcal{E}$ meet certain density criteria, with $|\mathcal{E}\cap[1,n]|$ exceeding $cn^k$ for all $n\geq 1$, then the size of $X$ necessary to remove almost all $\varepsilon$-fraction of the edges $\varepsilon|\mathcal{E}|$ scales according to $\varepsilon^{-1/(r-1)}$. This requirement directly relates to combinatorial problems within Ramsey theory. Our work complements research by Nagel, Nenadov, Skokan, and Tran, who identified the minimum size of $X$ needed to remove a constant fraction of edges in certain $\varepsilon$-free graphs, specifically those with uniform degrees and cliques.

Ontology visualization is crucial for comprehension, and OntoPlot is an advanced visualization technique designed to effectively showcase ontologies in Plotly. Plotly's interactive features provide a superior visual experience compared to traditional static visualization methods. However, the current OntoPlot implementation has certain limitations in representing complex, real-world ontologies, particularly their hierarchical nature. In response, a new ontology visualization approach, Entangled Ontology Visualization (EOV), has been developed to depict non-hierarchical relationships within ontologies and illustrated through a practical example in the medical domain.

We showcase cycle-consistent training as a multi-task approach to significantly improve semi-supervised Automated Speech Recognition across various speech datasets. This technique involves using a model that generates transcription outputs from speech inputs and a reciprocal model that creates synthetic speech inputs from desired inverse transcription outputs. Preserving distribution consistency through this cycle process enables a practice of using a large inverse dataset for training without requiring accurate alignment between input and output pairs. The proposed method has been successfully applied in speaker adaptation and now also shows great potential in data augmentation for ASR. This results in using unlabelled data more effectively for training compared to a baseline that only utilizes a few labeled examples, providing better performance with no additional cost.

This research focuses on developing an intelligent navigation system utilizing deductive reasoning for robot pathfinding, encompassing depicted segments, pose estimates, and navigational constraints within a dedicated language framework. Building upon the ProDeD framework, the system employs active learning strategies to address data scarcity challenges, alternating between model expansion and targeted data collection during training. A self-supervised approach to robust navigational rule acquisition is also introduced, enabling the system to execute autonomous navigation tasks based on derived rules. Furthermore, the system is applied to enable self-governing navigation in mobile robots and demonstrates potential for adaptation to diverse applications like autonomous driving and game AI agents, which will be explored in future studies.

A soft spherical particle within a temperature and concentration gradient experiences a force driving it towards the hotter region - the Soret force. This force is thought to be a result of interactions between the particle and its environment. Our research explores the possibility that internal structural changes contribute to this phenomenon in soft particles in a density and temperature gradient.

To better understand this phenomenon, we've created a precise theoretical model that considers a particle with a compressible surface layer suspended in an ideal fluid, and we've calculated how thermal fluctuations affect its shape.

By calculating how these shape fluctuations impact the particle's temperature profile, we've found that stiffer particles experience a stronger Soret effect than those with more flexible surfaces, specifically a Soret effect that weakens as the particle stiffness decreases.

Additionally, our findings suggest that thermal shape fluctuations can be observed through the diffusion of such particles and their resulting temperature profiles.

Recent advancements in Automatic Music Composition have seen increased focus on improving the quality of generated music. As a result, more comprehensive and fair evaluation metrics have been developed to better assess Automatic Music Composition. To create a more effective evaluation metric, we propose employing Transformer-based models, which can learn nuanced characteristics of training data, for automatic evaluation. Specifically, we suggest using a pretrained model, such as RoBERTa, to create a evaluator that facilitates automatic evaluation by fine-tuning on a newly established, more balanced dataset. The underlying music dataset was constructed by evaluating human-generated melodies against generated melodies, for various genres of music, utilizing a generated melody evaluation dataset that encompasses pop music.

Adaptation techniques are crucial in particle filters for mitigating target tracking issues resulting from detection errors. However, the number of false positives often hinders real-time implementation of these methods. This paper introduces an unsupervised technique for minimizing numerous false positives in particle filters without compromising target tracking accuracy. We utilize clustering to group similar target objects and reorganize the likelihood distribution of a particle filter, thereby reducing false positives. We assess our approach using Common Objects in Video and European Traffic Telemetry challenges to identify false positives resulting from camera detection errors. Furthermore, we integrate our approach with a particle filter target tracker and observe its efficacy in eliminating spurious target information.

We propose an integrated approach to elevate the quality of music recordings. 
To broaden the range of available processing methods, we incorporate a novel technique derived from unpaired image transformation. This technique is then combined with VOCODE, a cutting-edge VOCoding technique, to transform and enhance music. The goal of our proposed approach is not only to improve music quality but also to alter its style, a capability that proves particularly valuable in stylistic transfer applications. Through comparative experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method and highlight areas of future development.

The widespread use of virtual reality has significantly influenced our understanding of human motion, allowing for the exploration of its applications in both entertainment and therapy. Research has revealed the Wound-Down Effect, a phenomenon where a virtual ball seems to recoil slightly upon release, even when it doesn't make contact with the user. This effect is often attributed to release velocity and object mass. However, our study, FauxThrow, investigates the impact of error in the Point of Release (PoR) during throwing movements. Through a study involving 20 participants, we discovered that the Object Rebound Effect (ORE) can be predicted by considering virtual object mass, release velocity, and error in the Point of Release. This research has significant implications for the development of more realistic throwing simulations, as well as the design of VR applications such as therapeutic applications, sports training, and motion capture technology.

We introduce an innovative tree-formated decoding strategy using transformer models in neural machine translation. This strategy enhances our understanding of the target language by integrating predicted syntactic analysis into the decoding phase. Building on a novel transformer architecture that includes nested cross-attention, our method leverages syntax-aware information from predicted dependency parses to generate high-quality target language trees. As a result, we achieve improved syntax-preserving output without needing target language annotations. Furthermore, our method leads to a significant performance boost on NMT tasks by a complete model fine-tuning process. Ultimately, our approach facilitates a detailed target language reading of the translated tree-formated output.

Interstellar molecular formation and destruction processes are influenced by the binding energy quantum states at dust grain surfaces, and current astrochemical models rely on estimated values due to a lack of comprehensive experimental data. A new web-based platform, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, has been created to gather and share dust grain binding energy data for use in astrochemical research. By utilizing a simple two-body model and incorporating screening effects, our quantum chemical calculations provide accurate adsorption site predictions and binding energy distributions for small gas-phase species on amorphous water ice, ice cores, and full-sized molecules with a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon framework. To facilitate research, binding energy data for various species are available on the B.E.A.P. platform, and our study of experimental data reveals that real-world experiments align with our model's predictions for small molecules and accurate adsorption sites are predicted for larger molecules on dust grain surfaces.

In this paper, the multiplicative stochastic model is studied with a lower limit dependent on the sample's empirical distribution function, rather than the conventional constant lower limit. The model's outcomes indicate that this lower limit substitution yields a parameter's estimated standard error reduction under specific conditions of the function's shape. Additionally, the lower limit's effect on a parameter's weighted average estimator is also examined using a stochastic approximation method, and the resulting error reduction is assessed.

A novel approach is introduced to evaluate circuit depths in algorithms based on random Clifford quantum circuits. The 'shallow shades' method employs midrange Clifford gates in a history-mixed manner to perform low-depth calculations. These gate sequences are then projected using specific decomposition methods, yielding insights into the circuit's performance. The method's effectiveness in assessing deeper circuits is substantiated, including its application to the Grover algorithm and a two-qubit parity-finding circuit. Moreover, shallow shades is made available as an open-source classical tool in Python to assist with circuit optimization.

The reflection coefficient's $|k|$ behavior for the Davey-Stewartson II equations has been analyzed for $Q_{xx} = 2 \psi_{yy}$ with specific boundary conditions. The study covers both the case where $b > 0$ and where $b < 0$, respectively. For a bounded reflection coefficient R(k), the researchers found that as $|k| \to \infty$, specific asymptotic properties hold, including R(k) being O($|k|^{-2}$) and O($|k|^{-3/2}$), which are consistent but exhibit different rates of convergence. The case where R(k) is not bounded, however, revealed the R(k) behavior near the real axis near the origin to be similar to $|k|^{-3/2}$.

This research introduces the concept of sibylvariant modifications, a type of modification where self-consistent processes maintain integrity over time. These modifications, derived from sibylvariant algorithms, are self-updating procedures used for data analysis. We focus on self-updating text classification procedures and develop algorithms that can detect sibylvariant modifications even in the presence of potentially manipulated data. Two resilient classification methods, RobustGaussianProcess and RobustBST, are presented, which rely on sibylvariant modifications and can be applied to a wide range of problems, including outlier detection, with minimal changes.

A new, more efficient approach to learning meta has been developed with the goal of creating flexible control over knowledge representation, rather than relying on predefined, concealed assumptions. Utilizing a simple encoding technique for images, this novel meta-learning system can generate a range of useful knowledge representations and facilitate complex multi-step problem-solving in domains such as shape manipulation and reasoning with mathematical symbols. By demonstrating the flexibility of the controller, the agent can switch between different modes of knowledge representation as needed, effectively learning to handle symbolic and linear reasoning tasks. Results from experiments using a simulated environment have shown that this system can successfully tackle linear reasoning problems and accurately translate the language produced by the controller into standard logical formats for evaluation. Furthermore, initial experiments exploring the integration of this controller into neural networks have yielded promising results and also revealed potential for representing function compositions and temporal reasoning within the linear representation framework.

High-performance multilingual language models are becoming increasingly accessible, thanks to advancements such as multilingual pretraining and transfer learning. Nonetheless, the challenges associated with handling various language inputs and the significant resource requirements of deploying these models limit their practical use. To overcome these limitations, model compression methods such as quantization and distillation have garnered significant interest in the machine translating community. To assess the resilience of these knowledge distillation approaches, we evaluate their robustness in maintaining high translation quality, particularly in scenarios where training data is limited. Our findings reveal that while distillation is effective in lowering the barrier to implementing multilingual neural machine translation for languages with lower resources, its effectiveness is not consistently demonstrated. Notably, we found that when using quantization, which is surprisingly robust to changes in model architecture and training data, we were able to achieve state-of-the-art results for several languages.

In recent years, the study of combinatorial algebraic geometry has gained significant traction, with researchers developing innovative methods to tackle challenging problems. A new hypergroup approach is proposed, where solitary hypergraphs serve as the foundation. By applying algebraic methods to the Lagrangian function of a solitary hypergraph, one can gain insights into the structure of this novel hypergroup. Notably, certain properties of this hypergroup exhibit remarkable consistency, despite initial appearances of logical coherence.

In the realm of automatic image analysis, particularly for tasks like image segmentation, access to vast amounts of annotated data is often required. This is notably the case in medical analysis, where obtaining and annotating data is often a time-consuming and expensive process. In our study, we have successfully minimized reliance on labeled data for pneumonia segmentation by first applying an image enhancement technique that makes abnormal regions more distinct and aligns with the original dataset. Additionally, we have computed inverse operations to ensure consistency with the original data distribution. Four image enhancement methods were considered but yielded similar results. The modified images were then used to train a Convolutional Autoencoder for image restoration to remove unwanted marks while preserving abnormal features, followed by training a U-Net based segmentation network on these restored images after simple denoising. The developed approach has been tested on three datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements over prior art with existing labeled data. Specifically, we have observed Jaccard score enhancements of up to 6.7%, 9.0%, and 4.4% for a subset of the VQI dataset over respective state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we have successfully validated the approach using only a small subset of a dataset for comparison, demonstrating significant performance improvements.

Current methods for processing a single image involve extensive knowledge bases, extensive neural networks, and significant computational resources. We've developed an alternative approach that creates prompt templates from a word list and then carries out management tasks using this organized framework. We utilize GPT-3 to fill in the prompts and produce descriptive text for images. Our low-resource system is successful in producing descriptive text for images using a limited set of words and standardizing its output format. We further enhance our method by incorporating constraints to regulate the generated descriptions and format them accordingly. When compared to state-of-the-art models, our approach matches their performance in processing a single image task and also excels in answering questions based on those descriptions.

This research explores the Causal Theory of Damage, drawing on various disciplines. The proposed theory asserts that an event or phenomenon $X$ causes damage to an entity $Y$ when it disruptts $Y$'s functional operations. The work aims to categorize four types of interference: (1) Preventative, (2) Impairing the entity's existing capabilities, (3) Derogatory, and (4) Negating potential capabilities. The first two types of interference are extensively examined and numerous cases are analyzed from diverse fields, such as the impact of disease on the body, the effect of a weapon on a person, and the influence of a toxin on a person's health. The analysis of these examples is crucial in understanding the underlying causal mechanisms. Furthermore, the research discusses the distinction between impairing and negating potential capabilities, identifies challenges in demonstrating that a particular event has caused harm, and examines the issue of moral responsibility in the context of causal theories.

MMLSpark is an open-source framework that brings deep learning capabilities to Apache Spark and allows the integration of various Machine Learning and Deep Learning algorithms. It was developed to overcome the limitations of existing frameworks, which were limited in functionality and difficult to use in real-world scenarios. This paper discusses the primary features of MMLSpark, including its ability to scale across clusters and its support for collaborative filtering, multi-margin learning, end-to-end learning, and supervised learning for time series forecasting, as well as its end-to-end learning capability using AutoEncoder and Recurrent Neural Networks. It also highlights the framework's end-to-end learning ability in an annotation context, as well as its ability to handle imbalanced datasets, and finally mentions the availability of MMLSpark on AWS EMR. Lastly, the paper showcases the flexibility and extensability of MMLSpark, and demonstrates its ability to use various storage and input methods, as well as its ability to integrate with other Spark and Cloud services.

Our approach enables a language model to be taught the speaking voice of an individual through just two examples, without needing prior exposure to that person's speech. This can be applied across various说话人识别 tasks such as identifying speakers or transcribing their speech. This technique functions by augmenting the model's existing text tokens with a speaker-specific vector, computed through an attention mechanism, after initially processing two samples of that speaker's speech. When encountered with an unknown speaker, the model treats their identity as a new "language," allowing for effective speaker verification, clustering, and identification through simple optimization or manipulation of the model's text-layer parameters. Experiments using the LJSCHT dataset and a four-speaker play-reading script demonstrate that our approach either rivals or surpasses a competing method that requires significantly more dataset samples, while requiring a significantly smaller dataset for speaker verification compared to a conventional voice interpreter. Additionally, our approach enables clustering of speakers using only two samples, and we demonstrate its applicability to both identifying and clustering of speakers on the VCTK corpus.

This research introduces a novel framework combining a heat equation, a Guartin heat flux model, and active boundary source/sink conditions. The study establishes global existence and positivity for weak solutions. Notably, when heat production/exothermicity is considered as a boundary force, the system's solvability is intriguingly similar to interior heat sources, despite its different mathematical structure.

The integration of highly-variable renewable energy sources and consumer-driven electric vehicles into the power grid poses significant forecasting challenges. This paper focuses on probabilistic daily load variable prediction for low-voltage grids. A model developed in this study utilizes daily data and geographical information to generate probability distributions that can be adjusted for different levels of accuracy and lead times. This probabilistic model ensures load profile coverage and achieves a high average score for accuracy metrics while providing more detailed and longer-horizon forecasts compared to traditional methods. Additionally, this model's flexibility can be used to optimize its accuracy by incorporating the target accuracy level and available forecast time. The model's performance was tested and validated using real data from Belgium, demonstrating its ability to deliver accurate and adaptable forecasts.

The increasing popularity of machine learning in healthcare is outpacing the ability of existing models to accurately generalize in healthcare settings due to their inability to capture subtle differences in clinical environments. This challenge is exacerbated by data bias, which can lead to unreliable predictions and potentially harmful decisions when deployed. This technical report explores how domain expertise can be leveraged to develop bias-aware machine learning models through various real-world examples, with a particular emphasis on healthcare. An illustrative use case is provided, showcasing the integration of a hospital's clinical knowledge to create a machine learning model that is also hospital-specific. This report aims to serve as a technical reference for healthcare institutions and technology companies, facilitating the development of more reliable and accurate models.

The goal of medical image segmentation and lesion localization is critical for understanding the characteristics of COVID-19, which can be obtained from various imaging techniques such as X-rays and CT scans. Current research has largely relied on either a direct approach or transfer learning methods, both of which have their limitations when applied to a diverse range of datasets. The direct approach typically involves training deep models on specific, well-labeled data, while transfer learning methods have shown promising results on various datasets but have not been widely compared. An ideal approach should ensure consistent performance on different datasets without relying on extensive annotations or prior knowledge. To address this need, a novel weakly guided approach is proposed in this research, where the model's prediction is influenced by the observations of multiple experts. Each expert guides the model's lesion localization and segmentation independently without directly training it. Furthermore, an adaptive weakly guided loss function is designed to accommodate both training and inference stages. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on various datasets.

The automatic positioning and recognition of vertebrae in CT scans is a fundamental task in various medical applications, and accurate side-marker alignment is essential for subsequent processing by deep learning algorithms. Traditional methods for creating spines in 2D X-ray images are often challenging and time-consuming, leading to  a common assumption that CT scans are already side-marked and aligned. However, rectifying the spine in CT scans is often necessary, especially when dealing with scoliosis, and this process is even more challenging than in X-ray images due to the complex and less consistent appearances of vertebrae. In this study, a novel approach is proposed to correct the spine in CT scans in a single step, considering the inherent challenges of colinearity and concavity that confound traditional methods. By leveraging the unique characteristics of the problem, supervised learning can effectively correct spines in the axial and sagittal planes in a single step, outperforming traditional methods in various aspects. In addition to spine correction, this paper also introduces two techniques, specifically the use of bony structures and data augmentation, to address concavity issues in vertebrae, and demonstrates the efficacy of these techniques in improving the performance of accurate vertebrae localization and classification.

We're investigating how dynamical stabilization occurs when a cavity's two-level emitter experiences extreme interaction with intense, oscillating vacuum light. By applying a multi-pole J. J. Sakurai scattering theory to resonant electron interactions, we've created a comprehensive model to study the resonant electron-cavity system under extremely strong coupling conditions. We've found that under specific shifts in the electron-cavity system, this extreme coupling suddenly gives way to moderate strength. Furthermore, our analysis using unitary transformations and eigenstates reveals the vacuum-bare dipole continuum, which features a unique 'shadow pole' that suppresses linear damping and leads to a coherent-swap dynamics, which can persist for extended periods of time, even in the presence of strong external influences.

A key feature of compliant legged robots is their elastic actuators, which bring many benefits, such as enhanced stability, increased efficiency, and improved performance. Nevertheless, designing these elastic actuators and optimizing their performance pose significant challenges. This study introduces the concept of utilizing adjustable-compliance actuators in a passive dynamics-controlled quadruped robot and develops an effective framework for optimizing their natural frequencies and damping ratios to further minimize energy consumption and improve contact stability. Experimental results confirm that an adjustable compliance controller can successfully adapt to uneven terrain and automatically adjust foot placement, whereas an experiment showcased the successful execution of standing jumps in these elastic-controlled quadrupeds.

This study proposes a quantum version of the Euler-Lagrange equations, which serve as criteria for state purity at specific times given an initial condition. These quantum criteria offer a clear and mathematically simple way to identify times of reducibility and semi-classical evolutions, unsuitable for further normalization. By providing a set of equations, we demonstrate the continuous, real, and positive nature of the quantum divisibility times, as well as their dependence on the initial wave function and external factors like potentials or magnetic fields. Furthermore, the equations enable a practical method using approximate solutions to achieve high levels of accuracy.

A tiny version of magnetic flux tubes occurs in certain plasma environments, specifically the magnetopause and Q-shocks, at a particular stage where electrons stop providing pressure, marked by the breakdown of the Hall-MHD regime. A study was conducted using a collisionless plasma model in order to understand the dynamics of these magnetic structures at this precise moment when they become unstable and tear apart. The findings reveal that these magnetic structures oscillate in a particular way, with the frequency and amplitude depending on electron properties and the intensity of magnetic fields, and as such, the oscillations are essentially a result of interactions between these magnetic structure's internal dynamics and electron movements within its core.

Fashion image retrieval with textual descriptions is an increasingly significant challenge due to its fundamental role in facilitating effective human-computer interaction. Current approaches successfully bridge the gap between language and visual domains, focusing on the semantic level, where a query is translated into a similar image-based meaning. By doing so, retrieval systems can pull up images regardless of how they are arranged, enhancing flexibility. Nonetheless, this often results in retrieving visually identical items, ignoring the essential aspect of fashion images: their traits. To fully address this, we introduce FIDELITY, a novel technique designed to customize fashion image retrieval based on specific traits. It enables us to answer queries such as, "Retrieve red pants worn by women." This innovative approach involves two stages: training a flexible embedding network to adjust to specified traits and utilizing a similarity metric to compare text and learned visual feature representations. Evaluations conducted on standard fashion datasets demonstrate the efficacy of FIDELITY.

We develop a dual gradient ascent method to tackle linear regulatory problems that are ill-defined due to invalid solutions. Our approach leverages dual problems with unique solutions to utilize gradient-based optimization techniques. It's capable of navigating the entirety of the feasible solution space, not just localized regions. By using Fenchel-Young inequalities, we demonstrate the method's convergence when the dual function possesses a unique minimum. Additionally, we investigate its behavior in ill-posed scenarios where solution uniqueness is compromised, employing both theoretical analysis and machine learning applications to assess its performance.

The evaluation of depth maps from light field data relies heavily on assessing the accuracy of estimated expenses. An effective estimator should not only account for measurement errors but also consider errors resulting from occlusions in the data. Our approach introduces a new estimator that incorporates an indicator map that marks regions affected by occlusions in the data. As expenses climb, the accuracy of depth increases, allowing us to utilize the highest expense quantiles to refine the depth map, along with the estimated expense and occlusion maps. Our estimator can also automatically adjust thresholds for occlusion maps based on the evaluation expenses. Our experiments show that the comparator's performance matches or surpasses that of the designer's estimator.
Using the bilinear approach, we demonstrate that the Fokas-Lenells equation admits two distinct simple wave solutions expressed in terms of Bessel functions, obtained via the Fay trilinear identity.

We also investigate solutions to linear perturbations within this novel gravitational framework and derive equations analogous to those governing non-ribbons. These equations are used to derive the Hamilton operator and demonstrate that it matches a beta-deformed Hamilton operator from a non-conformal string theory in the large momentum limit. Additionally, we investigate whether non-ribbons can be derived from a non-conformal O($d^2$) fermion theory via a Schur function, and derive an equation analogous to YSE in the framework of non-ribbons. In order to improve the channel load conscious connectivity of IEEE 802.11 clients, 
particularly those, like home WiFi extensions, that associate with multiple APs, 
this paper proposes an enhancement to the IEEE 802.11u/w standards and the fast roaming mechanism defined in IEEE 802.11v/r. 
Specifically, this paper presents a novel capability, known as Channel Load Conscious Association (CLCA), 
which is distinct from roaming and allows a client to associate with an AP, 
such as a home WiFi extension, that supports virtual APs (VAPs), 
without actually authenticating and handshaking with it. 
CLCA leverages Channel Load Information (CLI), communicated by an AP, 
like a home WiFi extension, through Channel Switch Announcement (CSA) or Action-No Ack frames, 
to facilitate a non-associating association. 
When associated with an AP, like a main AP, a client listening to its associated Extender AP(s) can receive their respective CLI values, 
compare them to the current AP it is associated with, 
to determine the most suitable AP, like a home WiFi extension, to support CLCA, 
similar to the process a client performs when performing a roam.
